Virol","nlmid":"0113724"},"printPublicationDate":"2026-11-01"},"pubYear":"2026","pageInfo":"e0131626","abstractText":"Although viral antigenic evolution is shaped by the competing demands of immune evasion and receptor-binding fitness, the physical principles underlying divergent viral evolutionary dynamics remain poorly understood. Here, by integrating structural biology, deep mutational scanning, and genomic surveillance data, we show that receptor-binding geometry constrains the spatial coupling between antibody escape and intrinsic viral fitness. In SARS-CoV-2, the exposed convex Spike-ACE2 interface spatially overlaps dominant neutralizing epitopes with receptor-contact residues, producing a stringent fitness-evasion trade-off. Consequently, viable escape mutations are largely restricted to a narrow peripheral region surrounding the receptor-binding core. As population immunity progressively saturates this limited escape space, continued adaptation increasingly requires coordinated saltational remodeling of the receptor-binding interface. In contrast, the influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin binds the small sialic acid ligand through a recessed pocket architecture that partially separates dominant antibody pressure from receptor-binding fitness constraints. This topological decoupling permits continuous stepwise antigenic drift without requiring frequent remodeling of the core binding site. Building on these findings, we develop a lightweight geometry-based framework that accurately identifies receptor-competitive antigenic hotspots across divergent viruses. Together, our results support a general model in which receptor geometry and protein surface topology strongly bias accessible antigenic evolutionary trajectories.

Importance

Why some viruses evolve through gradual antigenic drift whereas others undergo recurrent evolutionary leaps remains a fundamental question in virology. By integrating protein structures, mutational scanning data, and genomic surveillance, we show that the geometry of the receptor-binding interface strongly influences how immune escape mutations affect viral fitness. In SARS-CoV-2, receptor-binding residues are highly exposed and overlap with dominant antibody targets, restricting immune escape to a narrow set of mutations and promoting periodic evolutionary leaps when this space becomes exhausted. In contrast, the receptor-binding pocket of influenza A virus H3N2 is partially shielded from antibody recognition, allowing continuous antigenic drift with fewer fitness constraints. We further demonstrate that these structural principles can be used to identify antigenic hotspots directly from virus-receptor complexes. These findings provide a mechanistic explanation for divergent viral evolutionary trajectories and offer a structural framework for studying and anticipating antigenic Background

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is prone to immune escape, and the synergistic mechanism of kynurenine, AhR, and EMT remains unclear.

Methods

TNBC cell lines and 4T1 orthotopic breast cancer mice were used for molecular, cellular, and in vivo intervention experiments.

Results

Kynurenine induced EMT in an AhR-dependent way, promoted cell migration and invasion, upregulated CCL2/CCL22, and inhibited the function of CD8⁺GrB⁺ T cells. Snail overexpression promotes H3K4me3 histone modification at IDO1 and TDO2 promoters to epigenetically amplify tryptophan metabolic enzyme expression. The AhR antagonist CH-223191 blocked the loop and reversed tumor immune escape.

Conclusion

ABSTRACT

While neuraminidase (NA) is emerging as a promising influenza vaccine target, it evolves rapidly and undergoes antigenic drift. However, our understanding of its evolutionary constraints remains limited. Here, we systematically quantified the replication fitness effects of >6,000 mutations for each of three antigenically diverse H1N1 NAs using deep mutational scanning. Moderate correlations among H1N1 NA fitness landscapes revealed mutations with strain-dependent replication fitness effects. Additionally, cross-subtype comparison between N1 and N2 NAs uncovered similar epistatic effects that were enriched in the C-terminal interprotomer interface. We also showed that NA mutational fitness strongly correlated between in vivo and in vitro . Characterization of 40 individually constructed NA mutants further demonstrated that NA mutational fitness depended more on its surface protein expression than on its total protein expression or endoplasmic reticulum stress induction. mutations over time and produced antigenic drift, leading to diminished serum neutralization and compromised vaccine efficacy. However, the structural basis underlying this divergence remains poorly defined. Herein, we observed that the newly emerging O/Cathay variants in China exhibited marked neutralization escape from porcine immune sera. Furthermore, using a panel of seven porcine-derived neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (pnAbs), we mapped two antigenic regions with crucial determinants responsible for neutralization escape in recent O/Cathay variants. The charge change at +2 residue (Q → H/R) downstream of the conserved RGD receptor-binding motif on VP1, which modulates sensitivity to multiple pnAbs (pO18-34, pO18-40 and pO18-43) and vaccine-induced sera. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of pO18-29 in complex with the ancient O/HN/CHA/93 strain and the recent variant O/18074 revealed a novel VP3-centered antigenic structure and showed that mutations at positions 73 (V → K) and 134 (K → T) on VP3 mediated neutralization escape in O/Cathay variants via disruption of hydrophobic interaction as well as the hydrogen bonds and salt bridge networks. Moreover, residues 73 and 134 synergistically regulate pnAbs (pO18-2, pO18-18, pO18-28 and pO18-29) recognition. Together, our findings elucidate structural basis of neutralizing evasion in O/Cathay FMDV and provide a molecular framework for the rational design of next-generation broad-spectrum FMDV vaccine against emerging O/Cathay variants.</p></abstract><abstract abstract-type="summary"><title>Author summary</title><p>Foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) remains a major threat to livestock production worldwide, and the emergence of new variants can undermine the effectiveness of existing vaccines. In this study, we examined newly emerging O/Cathay FMDV variants circulating in China and found that they can evade neutralization by immune sera from vaccinated pigs. By analyzing a panel of pig-derived neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, we identified two antigenic regions that play distinct roles in mediating this neutralization escape. A charge-changing mutation near the conserved RGD receptor-binding site on the viral capsid protein VP1 reduces antibody recognition. Cryo-electron microscopy structures further revealed a previously unrecognized antigenic surface on the VP3 protein. We show that mutations at positions 73 and 134 on VP3 disrupt critical molecular interactions, including hydrophobic contacts, hydrogen bonds, and salt bridges, thereby enabling the virus to escape multiple antibodies binding. Notably, these two residues on VP3 act cooperatively to regulate antibody recognition. Together, our findings provide structural insights into how emerging FMDV variants evade immune responses and highlight specific targets for the design of broadly protective vaccines against evolving O/Cathay strains.</p></abstract><funding-group><award-group id="award001"><funding-source>

sec-type="intro" id="sec001"><title>Introduction</title><p>Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious viral disease affecting cloven-hoofed animals, including pigs, cattle, and sheep, and poses a major threat to animal health and international trade [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref001" ref-type="bibr">1</xref>]. The causative agent, foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV), comprises seven immunologically distinct serotypes, with serotype O being the most prevalent and antigenically diverse [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref002" ref-type="bibr">2</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref003" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>]. In Asia, recent epidemics have primarily been caused by three topotypes of serotype O, including Middle East-South Asia (ME-SA), Southeast Asia (SEA), and Cathay (CHY) [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref004" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref005" ref-type="bibr">5</xref>]. Notably, Cathay topotype viruses have shown an accelerated evolutionary rate and increased genetic diversity in recent years, raising concerns about their ongoing antigenic variation [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref006" ref-type="bibr">6</xref>].</p><p>The Cathay topotype represents a distinct lineage of serotype O FMDV with unique biological and epidemiological features. Strains of Cathay topotype display a pronounced porcinophilic phenotype and harbor characteristic deletions in both the 5′ untranslated region (UTR) and the non-structural protein 3A gene [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref007" ref-type="bibr">7</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref008" ref-type="bibr">8</xref>]. Since its initial emergence in Hong Kong in the 1970s [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref009" ref-type="bibr">9</xref>], the O/Cathay lineage has repeatedly caused outbreaks in swine populations, including the large-scale epidemic in Taiwan in 1997 [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref010" ref-type="bibr">10</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref011" ref-type="bibr">11</xref>]. Over the decades, Cathay strains have continued to circulate across East and Southeast Asia, and diversified into multiple independently evolving sub-lineages [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref012" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>–<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref014" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>]. As a consequence of this sustained circulation and diversification, recent O/Cathay viruses have exhibited pronounced antigenic drift, leading to a marked reduction in the effectiveness of conventional vaccines [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref006" ref-type="bibr">6</xref>]. Vaccination remains the cornerstone of FMD prevention and control; however, the antigenic variation creates a major problem in controlling FMD outbreaks by using conventional inactivated virus vaccines [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref015" ref-type="bibr">15</xref>]. Although current serotype O inactivated vaccines effectively protect against ME-SA and SEA viruses, newly emerged O/Cathay variants exhibit markedly reduced antigenic match and frequently escape vaccine-induced neutralization [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref016" ref-type="bibr">16</xref>].</p><p>Antigenic drift in FMDV follows several key principles. Minimal structural changes, most commonly single amino acid substitutions in side chains that alter size or charge, can disrupt antibody binding without altering backbone conformation or compromising capsid integrity and function [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref017" ref-type="bibr">17</xref>]. These substitutions are spatially clustered and predominantly occur at five major surface-exposed antigenic sites (sites 1–5) located on the capsid proteins VP1, VP2, and VP3 [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref018" ref-type="bibr">18</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref019" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>]. Pronounced antigenic drift often involves co-variation, in which coordinated substitutions across multiple antigenic sites, particularly sites 1, 2, and 5, collectively remodel antigenic epitopes on FMDV capsids [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref020" ref-type="bibr">20</xref>]. Consistent with these principles, antigenic drift in O/Cathay viruses has been associated with substitutions at multiple antigenic residues. The substitutions in VP1 (positions 141, 147, and 149) and VP2 (position 130) contribute to immune escape [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref005" ref-type="bibr">5</xref>]. A VP2 S72N substitution was also identified as a key antigenic determinant in O/Penghu/2012 using a mouse-derived monoclonal antibody [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref021" ref-type="bibr">21</xref>]. However, most existing analyses rely on murine antibodies and lack structural resolution, limiting mechanistic insight into antibody recognition and escape in the natural porcine host.</p><p>In this study, we employed a panel of seven porcine-derived neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (pnAbs) to characterize the antigenic architecture of recent O/Cathay strains. We show that Cathay variants circulating between 2016 and 2022 exhibit substantial escape from neutralization by both porcine immune sera and monoclonal antibodies. We identify the key antigenic determinant of neutralization escape approaching the receptor binding region on VP1. Cryo-EM complex structures uncovered a previously uncharacterized VP3-centered conformational epitope and demonstrated a synergistic escape involving VP3 residues 73 and 134. These findings provide insights into the molecular mechanisms driving antigenic drift in O/Cathay variants and offer a structural framework for rational vaccine updates to improve protection in swine populations in Asia.</p></sec><sec sec-type="results" id="sec002"><title>Results</title><sec id="sec003"><title>The newly emerging O/Cathay variants exhibited marked neutralization escape from porcine immune sera</title><p>To evaluate the antigenic variation of the newly emerged O/Cathay strains (O/SCGH/CHA/2016, O/18074, O/GD/2021 and O/GX/2022) isolated between 2016 and 2022, cross-neutralization assays were performed using porcine sera from four distinct immunized groups. Each group consisted of ten pigs that had received two doses of inactivated vaccines containing 146S antigens derived from the O/HN/CHA/93 (Cathay), O/XJ/CHA/2017 (O/Ind/2001 lineage), O/Tibet/99 (O/PanAsia lineage), or O/GSLX/2010 (O/Mya98 lineage), respectively. Compared with the ancient O/HN/CHA/93 strain, all four O/Cathay variants exhibited substantial escape from serum neutralization across all immunized groups (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g001" ref-type="fig">Fig 1</xref>). In the O/HN/CHA/93-immunized group, the mean neutralizing titers against O/SCGH/CHA/2016, O/18074, O/GD/2021 and O/GX/2022 strains were decreased by 11.8-, 14.0-, 15.2- and 24.5-fold, respectively, relative to those against O/HN/CHA/93 strain (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g001" ref-type="fig">Fig 1A</xref>). A similar pattern was also observed in the O/Ind/2001-immunized group, with the lowest titers observed against O/GX/2022 strain, followed by O/GD/2021, O/18074 and O/SCGH/CHA/2016 strains (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g001" ref-type="fig">Fig 1B</xref>). In contrast, sera from pigs immunized with the O/Tibet/99 or O/Mya98 showed lower neutralization against the O/SCGH/CHA/2016 than against O/18074, whereas neutralization of O/GD/2021 and O/GX/2022 remained consistently low (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g001" ref-type="fig">Fig 1C</xref>-<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g001" ref-type="fig">D</xref>). The radar plot further highlights a pronounced decline in neutralizing titers against the four recent O/Cathay variants compared with those against O/HN/CHA/93 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g001" ref-type="fig">Fig 1E</xref>).</p><fig position="float" id="ppat.1014650.g001" orientation="portrait"><object-id pub-id-type="doi">10.1371/journal.ppat.1014650.g001</object-id><label>Fig 1</label><caption><title>Neutralization of O/Cathay variants by porcine sera.</title><p><bold>(A-D)</bold> The neutralization titers of ancient O/HN/CHA/93 strain and representative O/Cathay variants were determined by microneutralization assay using porcine sera collected from four different immunization groups vaccinated with four different serotype O virus antigens. The O virus antigens are O/HN/CHA/93 (Cathay), O/XJ/CHA/2017 (O/Ind/2001 lineage), O/Tibet/99 (O/PanAsia lineage), or O/GSLX/2010 (O/Mya98 lineage). The inactivated vaccine strains and the sample size (n) for each group are indicated in the panel titles. Fold changes in geometric mean neutralization titers against each variant relative to the O/HN/CHA/93 strain are indicated by symbols. Statistical differences between O/HN/CHA/93 and each O/Cathay variant were analyzed with one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett's multiple-comparison test in GraphPad Prism 7.2. ***P < 0.001; **P < 0.01; *P < 0.05. Experiments were performed independently in triplicate. <bold>(E)</bold> Radar plot showing the serum neutralization profiles for four immunized groups. Groups of three-month old healthy pigs (n = 10) were immunized with the indicated vaccine formulations.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="ppat.1014650.g001.webp"><?image-name ppat.1014650.g001.webp?><?image-size 114650?><?image-md5 cb90d69fb0c2a039e4ae8d9e828d7424?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 1165?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 1165?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/cb90d69fb0c2/ppat.1014650.g001.webp?><?thumb-name ppat.1014650.g001.gif?><?thumb-size 9729?><?thumb-md5 f8aeb226add6bfbeb8ee1746adbd05ef?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 146?><?thumb-scaled-width 200?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/f8aeb226add6/ppat.1014650.g001.gif?></graphic></fig><p>To further assess whether these findings extend to other topotypes of serotype O, we evaluated cross-neutralization of the recently emerged ME-SA (O/GZ1/2025) and SEA (O/HNNY/2022) strains using the same panel of porcine sera. Notably, the neutralization profiles of these two strains differed markedly from those of O/Cathay variants. O/HNNY/2022 escaped neutralization by O/HN/CHA/93 (4.7-fold), O/Tibet/99 (2.3-fold), and O/Ind/2001 (2.0-fold) sera (Fig A panels A-C in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>), but showed enhanced neutralization (0.6-fold) by O/Mya98 sera (Fig A panel D in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). In contrast, O/GZ1/2025 exhibited marginal escape from O/HN/CHA/93 (2.6-fold) and O/Mya98 (1.4-fold) sera, while displaying enhanced neutralization by O/Tibet/99 (0.9-fold) and O/Ind/2001 (0.8-fold) sera (Fig A in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Among the four vaccine groups, sera from pigs immunized with the O/Ind/2001 exhibited consistently higher neutralizing activity against all tested strains, indicating broader cross-reactivity.</p><p>Notably, phylogenetic analysis of the P1 region showed that O/Cathay variants from 2016–2022 formed a distinct clade, with O/GD/2021 and O/GX/2022 occupying the most divergent branches (Fig B panel A in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). This correlates directly with their rank order of neutralization resistance observed in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.g001" ref-type="fig">Fig 1</xref> (O/GX/2022 > O/GD/2021 > O/18074 > O/SCGH/CHA/2016), providing evidence that genetic drift in P1 is associated with progressive antigenic change within the Cathay topotype. Collectively, these results demonstrate that O/GX/2022 exhibits the greatest resistance to porcine serum neutralization, followed by other O/Cathay variants, highlighting increasing antigenic divergence within Cathay topotype.</p></sec><sec id="sec004"><title>Reduced binding and neutralization of O/Cathay variants were further confirmed by porcine monoclonal antibodies</title><p>We selected 55 mAb clones from the previously established O/18074-specific porcine BCR repertoire (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g002" ref-type="fig">Fig 2A</xref>) [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref012" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>], derived from a pig primed and boosted with O/HN/CHA/93 and then immunized with O/18074, O/Tibet/99, A/WH/CHA/09, and A/AF72. These clones were chosen based on high clonal frequency and somatic hypermutation (SHM) profiles and were derived from the unique 2014 O-specific clonotypes after excluding clonotypes shared with the serotype A repertoire. Seven representative porcine mAbs (designated as pO18-2, pO18-18, pO18-28, pO18-29, pO18-30, pO18-34 and pO18-43) were expressed for further analysis. The binding reactivity of these mAbs to the ancient O/Cathay strain O/HN/CHA/93 and the recent variant O/18074 was evaluated using indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) and biolayer interferometry (BLI). All mAbs recognized O/HN/CHA/93 in IFA, although with varying intensities (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g002" ref-type="fig">Fig 2B</xref>). PO18-2 and pO18-43 showed weak fluorescence signals, whereas the remaining mAbs displayed strong reactivity. All mAbs exhibited only weak binding to O/18074 in IFA (Fig C in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). BLI kinetic analyses revealed that all mAbs bound O/HN/CHA/93 with greater affinity than the recent variant O/18074 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g002" ref-type="fig">Fig 2C</xref>-<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g002" ref-type="fig">D</xref>), with slower dissociation rates observed for O/HN/CHA/93. Among them, pO18-28 showed the largest difference in affinity, with a dissociation constant (KD) of 0.246 nM for O/HN/CHA/93, and 11 nM for O/18074. PO18-29 exhibited the greatest difference in dissociation rate, with k_off values of 1.90 × 10<sup>−4</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> for O/HN/CHA/93, and 5.62 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−4</sup> for O/18074. pO18-43 showed a smaller difference than other mAbs, with an approximately threefold change in k_off value. Overall, all mAbs showed lower binding affinity to O/18074 than to O/HN/CHA/93 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g002" ref-type="fig">Fig 2E</xref>). The higher affinity of O/18074-derived mAbs for the ancient strain O/HN/CHA/93 than for the homologous variant is consistent with original antigenic sin [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref022" ref-type="bibr">22</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref023" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>], a phenomenon in which initial exposure to an ancestral strain shapes subsequent antibody responses toward cross-reactive epitopes.</p><fig position="float" id="ppat.1014650.g002" orientation="portrait"><object-id pub-id-type="doi">10.1371/journal.ppat.1014650.g002</object-id><label>Fig 2</label><caption><title>Functional characterization of porcine-derived monoclonal antibodies against FMDV.</title><p><bold>(A)</bold> Schematic diagram of selection and preparation of porcine mAbs from O/18074 strain-specific BCR repertoire. The immunoglobulin germline gene usage (VH, DH, JH, Vλ, Jλ) was identified and characterized. Frequency indicated the frequency of clonotypes for each mAb that appeared in O/18074-specific repertoire. SHM indicated frequency of replacement and silent mutations in full variable region sequence of heavy chain (VH), which was calculated by SHazaM using the program Immcantation.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="ppat.1014650.g002.webp"><?image-name ppat.1014650.g002.webp?><?image-size 346452?><?image-md5 69e800a95138f65e39d1a8b587dec2fc?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 1895?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 1895?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/69e800a95138/ppat.1014650.g002.webp?><?thumb-name ppat.1014650.g002.gif?><?thumb-size 17598?><?thumb-md5 9a98607935dd3987c43f1a3044083610?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 200?><?thumb-scaled-width 169?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/9a98607935dd/ppat.1014650.g002.gif?></graphic></fig><p>We then assessed neutralization breadth and potency of these mAbs using virus neutralization assay (VNT) against the representative epidemic strains of FMDV serotypes O circulating in China, including O/Tibet/99 and O/GZ1/2025 (ME-SA topotype), O/GSLX/2010 and O/HNNY/2022 (SEA topotype), and five strains (O/HN/CHA/93, O/SCGH/CHA/2016, O/18074, O/GD/2021 and O/GX/2022) in Cathay topotype as well as serotype A strains (A/AF72, A/WH/CHA/09, and A/GDMM/2013). All seven mAbs exhibited broad neutralizing activity against O/Tibet/99, O/GZ1/2025, O/GSLX/2010, O/HNNY/2022 and O/HN/CHA/93 strains in the VNT. In contrast, neutralizing activity of these mAbs was markedly reduced against Cathay variants isolated after 2016, with several mAbs completely losing neutralizing activity against O/GD/2021 and O/GX/2022. None of these mAbs could neutralize the tested FMDV serotype A strains.</p><p>Among these mAbs, pO18-2 demonstrated potent neutralizing activity against O/HN/CHA/93 (<1 μg/mL), but exhibited markedly weaker activity against O/SCGH/CHA/2016 (41.25 μg/mL) and O/18074 (46.67 μg/mL), and completely lost activity against O/GD/2021 and O/GX/2022 (>50 μg/mL) (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g002" ref-type="fig">Fig 2F</xref>). The broad neutralization profiles of these mAbs further indicate that the recently emerged ME-SA (O/GZ1/2025) and SEA (O/HNNY/2022) strains have not undergone significant antigenic variation. The reduced neutralization correlated with decreased binding affinity for the variants, underscoring the substantial antigenic variation that has emerged among O/Cathay strains after 2016.</p></sec><sec id="sec005"><title>The charge change at RGD + 2 position (Q → H) significantly affected antigenic variation and occurred in emerging variants of O/Cathay topotype</title><p>To illustrate key determinants of antigenic variation in O/Cathay strains emerging after 2016, we generated neutralization escape mutants against the seven pnAbs using the O/HN/CHA/93 strain as the parental virus. As summarized in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.t001" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>, escape mutations were mapped to VP1 for three pnAbs, whereas mutations selected by the remaining four pnAbs localized in VP3. Escape mutants selected by pO18-34, pO18-40, and pO18-43 harbored substitutions within the VP1 G-H loop. Notably, these substitutions clustered downstream of the RGD motif, which constitutes the integrin receptor-binding site of FMDV. A total of 24 mutants contained substitutions at VP1 position 149 (RGD + 2). Most substitutions (14/24) involved a change from glutamine (Q) to arginine (R), with additional substitutions to lysine (K), histidine(H), or leucine (L) (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.t001" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>). Sanger sequencing of the escape mutants confirmed the presence of these mutations in the viral stocks (Figs D-F in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). We further performed amplicon sequencing to quantify the mutation frequency in the viral stocks. For three representative escape mutants (one each for pO18-34, pO18-40, and pO18-43), all three exhibited mutations at P1 position 2015 (corresponding to VP1 residue 149), with a mutation frequency exceeding 90% (Fig G in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). For the pO18-43 escape mutant, additional mutations were detected at P1 positions 489, 819, and 135, which were synonymous and present at frequencies below 1%. Interestingly, these substitutions predominantly altered amino acid charge or polarity, and the majority represented a shift from neutral to basic residues. Sequence alignment of FMDV serotype O viruses revealed a consistent residue difference at VP1 position 149 between ancient and recent strains. The ancient O/HN/CHA/93 strain carries Q149, whereas O/Cathay variants after 2016 predominantly carry H149 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g003" ref-type="fig">Fig 3A</xref>).</p><table-wrap position="float" (n = 215 full-length VP1 sequences) retrieved from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database as of January 14, 2026.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="ppat.1014650.g003.webp"><?image-name ppat.1014650.g003.webp?><?image-size 204864?><?image-md5 63836c777a64befd6ebd01c341d5fa50?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 1590?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 1590?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/63836c777a64/ppat.1014650.g003.webp?><?thumb-name ppat.1014650.g003.gif?><?thumb-size 16816?><?thumb-md5 4088376babd8dc8a41fc08541a5d3663?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 199?><?thumb-scaled-width 200?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/4088376babd8/ppat.1014650.g003.gif?></graphic></fig><p>To further validate the functional relevance of this residue, recombinant viruses bearing VP1 residue 149 substitutions were rescued and confirmed by Sanger sequencing and plaque assays (Fig H in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>), and subsequently assessed for their sensitivity to neutralization by three pnAbs individually. In the O/HN/CHA/93 background, introduction of Q149H substitution completely abolished neutralization by pO18-34, pO18-40, and pO18-43 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g003" ref-type="fig">Fig 3B</xref>). Accordingly, the reciprocal H149Q substitution in O/18074 background markedly restored neutralization by all these pnAbs (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g003" ref-type="fig">Fig 3C</xref>). Next, we assessed the impact of this substitution on polyclonal antibody responses <italic toggle="yes">in vivo</italic>, and sera from O/HN/CHA/93-immunized pigs were examined in cross-neutralization assays against the recombinant viruses of O/HN/CHA/93 with Q149H substitution (<sub>OHN-VP1</sub>Q149H) and O/18074 with H149Q substitution (<sub>O18-VP1</sub>H149Q) mutant viruses. No obvious difference in neutralizing antibody titers was observed between the porcine sera against the WT strain and the <sub>OHN-VP1</sub>Q149H mutant (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g003" ref-type="fig">Fig 3D</xref>). However, neutralizing antibody titers to <sub>O18-VP1</sub>H149Q mutant virus were significantly higher than those against parental virus O/18074 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g003" ref-type="fig">Fig 3E</xref>). These results consolidate that VP1 residue 149 (RGD + 2) plays a pivotal role in modulating monoclonal antibody recognition and exerts a substantial influence on polyclonal serum neutralization.</p><p>Consistent with these functional observations, global sequence analyses revealed a clear temporal shift at VP1 residue 149 (RGD + 2) in O/Cathay viruses, evolving with time from glutamine (Q) in ancient strains to arginine (R), and predominantly histidine (H), in more recent variants (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g003" ref-type="fig">Fig 3F</xref>-<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g003" ref-type="fig">G</xref>). Collectively, these findings establish VP1 residue 149 (RGD + 2) as a key determinant of antibody recognition and a major antigenic site in recent O/Cathay strains.</p></sec><sec id="sec006"><title>Cryo-EM complex structures of virus-antibody revealed novel antigenic regions on VP3, with similar antigen footprints, but different numbers of hydrogen bonds and salt bridge networks between the ancient strain and variant in O/Cathay topotype</title><p>Escape mutants selected by pO18-2, pO18-18, pO18-28, and pO18-29 all harbored substitutions in VP3 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.t001" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>). None of these four pnAbs bound to denatured viral antigens by WB, indicating that they recognize conformational epitopes on surface of viral capsid. To dissect the structural basis of neutralization escape in emerging O/Cathay variants, we selected pO18‑29 for cryo‑EM analysis, as it exhibited potent neutralization against the ancestral O/HN/CHA/93 strain but not against the recent variants (2016–2022). We resolved cryo-EM structures of the pO18-29 single-chain variable fragment (scFv) in complex with capsids from the ancient strain O/HN/CHA/93 (FMDV-OHN–pO18-29) and the recent variant O/18074 (FMDV-O18–pO18-29), respectively. In both reconstructions, 60 copies of the scFv were symmetrically arranged around the threefold axes of the viral capsid (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g004" ref-type="fig">Fig 4A</xref>-<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g004" ref-type="fig">B</xref>). The final reconstructions reached resolutions of 2.24 Å for FMDV-OHN–pO18-29 and 2.34 Å for FMDV-O18–pO18-29, as estimated by the 0.143 FSC criterion (Fig I in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>), enabling reliable atomic modeling of the FMDV capsid proteins and the variable loops of the scFv antibody. Structural superposition of the two complexes yielded an RMSD of 1.432 Å (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g004" ref-type="fig">Fig 4C</xref>), indicating that antibody engagement adopts a nearly identical global architecture in both strains. The two complexes exhibited highly similar overall antigenic footprints (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g004" ref-type="fig">Fig 4D</xref>-<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g004" ref-type="fig">E</xref>). The buried surface areas were comparable (1089.63 Å² for O/HN/CHA/93 versus 1005.04 Å² for O/18074) (Tables A and B in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>).</p><fig position="float" id="ppat.1014650.g004" orientation="portrait"><object-id pub-id-type="doi">10.1371/journal.ppat.1014650.g004</object-id><label>Fig 4</label><caption><title>Cryo-EM analysis of the FMDV-OHN-pO18-29 and FMDV-O18-pO18-29 complexes.</title><p><bold>(A, B)</bold> The central cross sections, rendered images, and antibody footprints of the FMDV-OHN-pO18-29 complex <bold>(A)</bold> and the FMDV-O18-pO18-29 complex <bold>(B)</bold>. The central cross sections of the cryo-EM maps are shown with icosahedral 2-, 3-, and 5-fold axes (Scale bar, 10 nm). In the rendered images, depth cueing with color is used to indicate the radius (< 100 Å, blue; 120–160 Å, from cyan to yellow; > 180 Å, red). The icosahedral 5- and 3-fold axes are represented by pentagons and triangles, respectively. Footprints of pO18-29 on the FMDV surface were produced using RIVEM [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref054" ref-type="bibr">54</xref>]. <bold>(C)</bold> Structural superposition of the FMDV-OHN–pO18-29 and FMDV-O18–pO18-29 complexes, aligned based on the FMDV capsid. The heavy and light chains of pO18-29 are colored cyan and magenta, respectively. Capsid proteins VP1, VP2, VP3, and VP4 are colored blue, green, red, and yellow, respectively. The all-atom root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of pO18-29 is 1.432 Å, and the backbone RMSD is 1.175 Å. <bold>(D, E)</bold> Footprint maps of residues within 4 Å of the antibody with FMDV-OHN-pO18-29 <bold>(D) or</bold> FMDV-O18-pO18-29 <bold>(E)</bold> within 4 Å. Residues are colored according to physicochemical properties: H, K, and R, positive (blue); D and E, negative, hydrophilic (red); S, T, N, and Q, neutral, hydrophilic (green); A, V, L, I, and M, aliphatic, hydrophobic (gray); F, Y, and W, aromatic (purple); P and G, proline and glycine (orange). The antibody interface is outlined by a black contour line.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="ppat.1014650.g004.webp"><?image-name ppat.1014650.g004.webp?><?image-size 639990?><?image-md5 85e1bc6b00a1484de786b9626f9c4ee7?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 2193?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 2193?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/85e1bc6b00a1/ppat.1014650.g004.webp?><?thumb-name ppat.1014650.g004.gif?><?thumb-size 16323?><?thumb-md5 a6f754a57945bd2c93cf22fdfb0381dd?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 200?><?thumb-scaled-width 146?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/a6f754a57945/ppat.1014650.g004.gif?></graphic></fig><p>Despite this conserved global footprint, the underlying intermolecular interaction networks differed markedly in composition and organization. In the FMDV-OHN–pO18-29 complex, pO18-29 engaged VP3 using residues from both heavy and light chains, forming an extensive interaction network comprising 17 hydrogen bonds and 5 salt bridges (Table C in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). These interactions involved residues in VP3 B-B knob (OHN-VP3E58), B-C loop (OHN-VP3D69, OHN-VP3S70, and OHN-VP3D71), βC (OHN-VP3Q76), and E-F loop (OHN-VP3E131 and OHN-VP3K134) interacting with residues in the CDRs and FRs of pO18-29, ordinal HCDR3(VHR102, VHR103, VHN105, VHG107, VHY110, VHY108, VHR111, and VHD112), HCDR1(VHY32), LCDR2(VLG51and VLD53), LCDR1(VLY33), L-FR3(VLR55 and VLN54), and L-FR2(Y50) (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g005" ref-type="fig">Fig 5A</xref>-<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g005" ref-type="fig">D</xref>). By contrast, although pO18-29 recognized a largely overlapping surface on the O/18074 capsid, the FMDV-O18–pO18-29 complex exhibited a reconfigured interaction network, characterized by 25 hydrogen bonds and 7 salt bridges at the interface (Table D in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). The residues in VP3 B-B knob (O18-VP3E58), B-C loop (O18-VP3T68, O18-VP3D69, O18-VP3S70, and O18VP3D71), βC (O18-VP3K73 and O18-VP3Q76), C-D loop(O18-VP3H85), E-F loop (O18-VP3E131 and O18-VP3P132), and VP1 C-terminus(O18-VP1A199) participated in contacts with pO18-29, including HCDR3(VHR103, VHN105, VHY110, VHY116, VHG107, and VHY108), HCDR1(VHN31), LCDR2(VLG51and VLD53), L-FR3(VLR55, VLR61 and VLN54), and L-FR2(Y50) (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g005" ref-type="fig">Fig 5E</xref>-<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g005" ref-type="fig">H</xref>). These data reflected a redistribution of intermolecular interactions rather than an expansion of the antigenic footprint.</p><fig position="float" id="ppat.1014650.g005" orientation="portrait"><object-id pub-id-type="doi">10.1371/journal.ppat.1014650.g005</object-id><label>Fig 5</label><caption><title>Structural basis of pO18-29 recognition.</title><p><bold>(A, E)</bold> Cartoon representations of the interaction interfaces between pO18-29 scFv and the capsids of O/HN/CHA/93 <bold>(A)</bold> and O/18074 <bold>(E)</bold>. The heavy chain and light chain of pO18-29 are colored cyan and magenta, respectively. Capsid proteins VP1 to VP4 are colored blue, green, red and yellow, respectively. <bold>(B-D)</bold> Expanded views of antibody–antigen interface highlight the VP3 E-F loop and βC <bold>(B)</bold>, B-C loop <bold>(C)</bold>, and B-B knob region <bold>(D)</bold> of O/HN/CHA/93. <bold>(F-H)</bold> Expanded views of antibody–antigen interface highlight the VP3 E-F loop and βC <bold>(F)</bold>, B-C loop <bold>(G)</bold>, and B-B knob region <bold>(H)</bold> of O/18074. Putative hydrogen bonds and salt bridges are indicated by black and orange dashed lines, respectively. Hydrophobic interactions are depicted as gray spheres.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="ppat.1014650.g005.webp"><?image-name ppat.1014650.g005.webp?><?image-size 394576?><?image-md5 532897803ce51871caf02cfce0da038b?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 2271?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 2271?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/532897803ce5/ppat.1014650.g005.webp?><?thumb-name ppat.1014650.g005.gif?><?thumb-size 16424?><?thumb-md5 029b525f01ac8a983859a95f1e5733ca?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 200?><?thumb-scaled-width 141?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/029b525f01ac/ppat.1014650.g005.gif?></graphic></fig><p>Consistent with this interpretation, energetic analysis revealed that, despite similar buried surface areas, the O/HN/CHA/93 complex exhibited higher stabilization and hydrogen-bonding energies than the O/18074 complex (Table E in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). This energetic disparity could be primarily attributed to two local structural differences at the interface (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g005" ref-type="fig">Fig 5</xref>). First, VP3 residue K134 in O/HN/CHA/93 formed both hydrogen bonds and salt bridges with pO18-29, whereas the corresponding residue in O/18074 (T134) lacked the positively charged side chain required for salt-bridge formation and instead participated mainly in weaker polar or van der Waals interactions. Second, VP3 residue V73 in O/HN/CHA/93 established a deep hydrophobic interaction with the HCDR3 loop of pO18-29 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g005" ref-type="fig">Fig 5B</xref>), serving as a key anchoring point. This hydrophobic contact was abolished in O/18074 due to the V73K substitution (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g005" ref-type="fig">Fig 5F</xref>), resulting in destabilization of the antibody-capsid interface. Collectively, these findings suggest that neutralization escape in the O/18074 variant is driven by subtle remodeling of hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions, leading to reduced interfacial stability without altering the overall antigenic footprint.</p></sec><sec id="sec007"><title>Synergistic mutations at positions 73 (V → K) and 134 (K → T) on VP3 mediate neutralization escape in O/Cathay variants via disruption hydrophobic interaction as well as the hydrogen bonds and salt bridge networks</title><p>Cryo-EM analysis revealed that pO18-29 engages a similar antigenic surface on VP3 in both the ancient strain O/HN/CHA/93 and the recent O/Cathay variant O/18074. However, the interaction networks differ. In the O/HN/CHA/93 complex, VP3 residues V73 and K134 formed a dense network of hydrophobic contacts, hydrogen bonds, and salt bridges with the antibody. In contrast, these interactions were substantially weakened in the O/18074 complex due to the V73K and K134T substitutions (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g006" ref-type="fig">Fig 6A</xref>), suggesting that residues 73 and 134 may act as key structural determinants of neutralization escape in O/Cathay variants. Consistent with their potential role in neutralization escape, sequence analysis revealed that the V73K substitution became increasingly prevalent among O/Cathay variants after 2015 (Fig B panel B in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>), while the K134T substitution showed a marked increase in prevalent strains after 2010 (Fig B panel C in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>).</p><fig position="float" id="ppat.1014650.g006" orientation="portrait"><object-id pub-id-type="doi">10.1371/journal.ppat.1014650.g006</object-id><label>Fig 6</label><caption><title>Key VP3 determinants in O/Cathay variants.</title><p><bold>(A)</bold> Sequence alignment of VP3 from ancient and variant O/Cathay strains. Residues at positions 73 and 134 are highlighted by blue box. <bold>(B, C)</bold> Neutralizing activity of pO18-29 against wild-type O/HN/CHA/93 (OHN-wt) <bold>(B)</bold> or wild-type O/18074 (O18-wt) <bold>(C)</bold> and the corresponding VP3 mutant viruses, measured using microneutralization assay. The neutralization concentration represented the lowest antibody concentration required to fully prevent CPE. <bold>(D, E)</bold> Neutralizing activity of pnAbs (pO18-2, pO18-28, and pO18-18) against wild-type O/HN/CHA/93 (OHN-wt) <bold>(D)</bold> or wild-type O/18074 (O18-wt) <bold>(E)</bold> and the corresponding VP3 mutant viruses, measured using microneutralization assay. Statistical differences between wild-type and mutant viruses were analyzed using an unpaired <italic toggle="yes">t</italic> test with the Holm–Sidak method (α = 0.05). ***P < 0.001; **P < 0.01; *P < 0.05; NS, not significant. Experiments were performed independently in triplicate.</p></caption><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="ppat.1014650.g006.webp"><?image-name ppat.1014650.g006.webp?><?image-size 204240?><?image-md5 66e8610a1012fe17e687216a05430b17?><?image-image-server-status NEED_LOADING?><?image-original-height 2492?><?image-original-width 1600?><?image-scaled-height 2492?><?image-scaled-width 1600?><?image-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/66e8610a1012/ppat.1014650.g006.webp?><?thumb-name ppat.1014650.g006.gif?><?thumb-size 9043?><?thumb-md5 46aaad4adac0a28348843bc074f2fba8?><?thumb-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?thumb-scaled-height 200?><?thumb-scaled-width 128?><?thumb-cloudpmc-urn urn:cdn:blobs/7418/13671523/46aaad4adac0/ppat.1014650.g006.gif?></graphic></fig><p>To functionally validate this hypothesis, we generated recombinant viruses carrying single or double substitutions at VP3 residues 73 and 134 (<sub>OHN-VP3</sub>V73K, <sub>OHN-VP3</sub>K134T, <sub>OHN-VP3</sub>V73K/K134T, <sub>O18-VP3</sub>K73V, <sub>O18-VP3</sub>T134K and <sub>O18-VP3</sub>K73V/T134K) using O/HN/CHA/93 and O/18074 infectious clones. All recombinant viruses were successfully rescued and confirmed by Sanger sequencing and plaque assays (Fig J in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). In the O/HN/CHA/93 background, the V73K substitution markedly reduced neutralization by pO18-29, whereas the K134T substitution alone had minimal effect (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g006" ref-type="fig">Fig 6B</xref>). Analysis of additional pnAbs revealed antibody-specific sensitivity patterns. Either the V73K or K134T substitution reduced neutralization by pO18-28, while the combined V73K/K134T mutation impaired neutralization by pO18-2, and the K134T substitution selectively reduced neutralization by pO18-18 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g006" ref-type="fig">Fig 6D</xref>). Notably, in the O/18074 background, the reciprocal K73V or T134K substitutions markedly enhanced neutralization by all four pnAbs, with the combined K73V/T134K substitutions producing the strongest restoration of sensitivity (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.g006" ref-type="fig">Fig 6C</xref> and <xref rid="ppat.1014650.g006" ref-type="fig">6E</xref>). Together, these results identify VP3 residues 73 and 134 as dominant and synergistic determinants of monoclonal antibody-mediated neutralization in O/Cathay strains.</p><p>To assess whether these substitutions broadly affected polyclonal sera neutralization, sera from pigs immunized with O/HN/CHA/93 were tested against the recombinant viruses. Neither introduction of the V73K, K134T, or V73K/K134T substitutions in the O/HN/CHA/93 background nor the reciprocal K73V, T134K, or K73V/T134K substitutions in the O/18074 background significantly altered serum neutralization compared with the respective parental viruses (Fig K in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). These findings indicate that VP3 residues 73 and 134 primarily modulate monoclonal antibody recognition and do not substantially affect polyclonal serum neutralization.</p><p>In addition to these fixed escape determinants, analysis of neutralization escape mutants selected by pO18-2, pO18-18, pO18-28, and pO18-29 revealed further substitutions clustered in VP3 (<xref rid="ppat.1014650.t001" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>). Escape mutants of pO18-18 predominantly carried double substitutions at residues 71 and 134 (4/8) or 70 and 134 (2/8), with single substitutions at either position being rare (1/8 each). Sanger sequencing of the escape mutants confirmed the presence of these mutations in the viral stocks (Fig L panel A in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Amplicon sequencing of one representative double mutant further revealed an additional substitution at VP3 residue 70 (Q → R) with a mutation frequency of 0.225 (Fig L panel B in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Sequence alignment confirmed divergence at VP3 residue 134 between O/HN/CHA/93 and circulating O/Cathay variants, while residue 71 remained highly conserved (Fig M panel A in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Recombinant viruses carrying single and the combined mutations at positions 71 and 134 were successfully rescued in the O/HN/CHA/93 background (Fig M panels B-C in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Functional analysis showed that the D71N substitution alone did not affect neutralization by pO18-18, while the K134T substitution markedly reduced neutralization, the combined D71N/K134 mutations completely escape neutralization by pO18-18 (Fig M panel D in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>).</p><p>Escape mutants selected by pO18‑2 and pO18‑28 exhibited diverse mutation profiles, with substitutions at VP3 residues 70, 76, and 134 appearing most frequently. In contrast, escape mutants selected by pO18-29 consistently carried substitutions at VP3 residues 70 and 76, most frequently in the form of double substitutions (S70P/Q76R, S70L/Q76R, or S70A/Q76R). Sanger sequencing of the escape mutants confirmed the presence of these mutations in the viral stocks (Figs N-P in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Amplicon sequencing of a pO18‑2 escape mutant carrying Q76R revealed additional mutations at VP3 residue 134 (K → E, 0.333; K → T, 0.414). Representative pO18‑28 and pO18‑29 mutants were also confirmed by amplicon sequencing, with only low‑frequency variants (<1%) detected at other positions (Fig Q in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Recombinant viruses bearing single or combined mutations at positions 70 and 76 were generated and successfully rescued in the O/HN/CHA/93 background (Fig R panels A-B in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Single substitutions at residue 70 had no detectable effect on neutralization, while the Q76R substitution conferred partial escape, and the combined S70P/Q76R substitution completely abolished neutralization by pO18-2 and pO18-29(Fig R panel C in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Despite their functional impact <italic toggle="yes">in vitro</italic>, residues 70 and 76 remained fully conserved among O/HN/CHA/93 and circulating O/Cathay variants (Fig R panel D in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>). Together, these data indicate that synergistic mutations facilitate escape from antibody neutralization. The VP3 residues 73 and 134 represent the dominant determinants of antigenic variation in circulating O/Cathay strains, whereas substitutions at residues 70 and 76 contribute to escape only under <italic toggle="yes">in vitro</italic> selective pressure.</p></sec></sec><sec sec-type="conclusions" id="sec008"><title>Discussion</title><p>In this study, we demonstrated that recent O/Cathay variants exhibit pronounced neutralization escape from multiple serotype O vaccine-induced sera as well as seven host-derived monoclonal neutralizing antibodies. We identified two spatially and mechanistically distinct antigenic regions on the viral capsid that contribute to antigenic variation and neutralization escape of O/Cathay viruses. The crucial antigenic determinant, located at residue 149 (RGD + 2) on the VP1 G-H loop downstream of the conserved RGD receptor-binding motif, modulates neutralization by pnAbs and vaccine-induced sera. In parallel, cryo-EM analysis uncovered a previously uncharacterized antigenic structure mapped to the βC and E-F loops of VP3. The key determinants, residues 73 (V → K) and 134 (K → T), mediate neutralization escape by perturbing hydrophobic contacts and reorganizing hydrogen bond and salt bridge networks. These two residues act synergistically to regulate pnAbs recognition. Comparable immune escape strategies driven by subtle electrostatic and structural remodeling at antibody-binding interfaces have also been reported in other RNA viruses, such as SARS-CoV-2 [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref024" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref025" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>] and enteroviruses [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref026" ref-type="bibr">26</xref>].</p><p>FMDV VP1 is a highly variable and immunogenic protein and contains the integrin-binding RGD motif within the G-H loop [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref027" ref-type="bibr">27</xref>]. As the most conformationally flexible region on the viral surface, the VP1 G-H loop plays a central role in receptor engagement and antigenic variation [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref028" ref-type="bibr">28</xref>]. Amino acid substitutions within the VP1 G-H loop can markedly alter viral antigenicity and promote escape from neutralizing antibodies [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref029" ref-type="bibr">29</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref030" ref-type="bibr">30</xref>]. Residues flanking the RGD motif are particularly critical for neutralization sensitivity, and coordinated changes at the RGD + 1, RGD + 2 or RGD + 3 positions contribute to fine-tuning the local conformation of the G-H loop [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref012" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref031" ref-type="bibr">31</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref032" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>]. Such substitutions can modulate antibody recognition without severely compromising viral fitness, underscoring their importance in immune-driven selection [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref012" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref033" ref-type="bibr">33</xref>]. Our study identified that the Q149H substitution (RGD + 2) completely abolished neutralization by pnAbs pO18-34, pO18-40, and pO18-43. Reversion of this residue to the ancient amino acid (H149Q) restored sensitivity to serum neutralization. Notably, the Q149H substitution introduces changes in amino acid polarity that are likely to destabilize local loop conformations, thereby altering antigen-antibody interactions. Together, these findings highlight the RGD + 2 position as a critical determinant shaping the antigenic architecture of VP1 and facilitating immune evasion in O/Cathay lineages.</p><p>Among the ﬁve known antigen sites of FMDV serotype O, site 4 was deﬁned by mutations at positions 56 and 58 on the VP3 B-B knob by both murine [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref034" ref-type="bibr">34</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref035" ref-type="bibr">35</xref>] and bovine [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref036" ref-type="bibr">36</xref>] mAbs. Subsequently, a novel antigenic site on VP3, including the βB (T65), B-C loop (T68), E-F loop (E131 and K134), and H-I loop (G196), was identified and shown to be functionally independent of antigenic site 4 by bovine mAbs (C4 and C4-like antibodies) [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref037" ref-type="bibr">37</xref>]. In our study, we further employed cryo-EM to resolve a previously unrecognized antigenic epitope on VP3, with key residues located at βC (73) and E-F loop (134). Notably, these residues exhibited synergistic effects in mediating neutralization escape of Cathay variants from pnAbs. These changes on VP3 are expected to reduce antibody affinity rather than abolish binding entirely. The cluster’s role as a thermodynamic anchor maximizes the benefit of both van der Waals contacts and the surrounding hydrogen-bond network. In contrast, the mutant interface of O/18074, reliant solely on an increased number of hydrogen bonds without the advantage of a desolvated core, achieves lower affinity due to the energetic penalty associated with hydrogen bond formation in a hydrated environment [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref038" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>,<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref039" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>].</p><p>Viral antigenic evolution or drift is driven by the continual emergence of variants capable of evading the existing immune response [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref040" ref-type="bibr">40</xref>]. This process reflects a balance between immune selection, structural constraints, and viral fitness [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref041" ref-type="bibr">41</xref>]. Escape mutations selected in vitro may not fully recapitulate those arising during natural infection; nevertheless, they delineate structurally and antigenically permissible evolutionary trajectories under sustained antibody pressure. Notably, although VP3 residues 70 and 76 are conserved between the ancient O/HN/CHA/93 strain and currently circulating Cathay variants, our mutagenesis data demonstrated that substitutions at these positions can cooperatively mediate escape from antibody neutralization. These findings suggest that this region constitutes a latent antigenic site that is structurally permissive to escape mutations, even though such changes have not yet been fixed in natural populations. Continued immune pressure may therefore unmask the antigenic relevance of this region during future viral evolution.</p><p>In summary, this study defines key molecular and structural determinants underlying antigenic variation in the O/Cathay topotype of FMDV. Our findings indicate that substitutions in VP1 and VP3 can reshape dominant neutralizing epitopes and promote immune escape without overt loss of viral viability. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding ongoing antigenic drift in porcinophilic FMDV strains and offer important insights for rational vaccine updating to improve protection against emerging O/Cathay variants in swine populations. Specifically, the identification of VP1 residue 149 (RGD + 2) and VP3 residues 73 and 134 as critical determinants of neutralization escape provides clear targets for monitoring antigenic drift in the field, potentially guiding strain selection for conventional vaccine updates. In addition, the structural characterization of these epitopes may facilitate the design of subunit immunogens that help broaden vaccine‑induced immunity.</p></sec><sec sec-type="materials|methods" id="sec009"><title>Materials and methods</title><sec id="sec010"><title>Expression and purification of porcine-derived mAbs</title><p>The selected paired VH and VL genes were synthesized with codon optimization and respectively cloned into porcine heavy chain (CH-pcDNA3.4) and light chain (Cκ-pcDNA3.4 or Cλ-pcDNA3.4) expression vectors to obtain the antibody-expressing plasmids VH-CH-pcDNA3.4 and VL-Cκ-pcDNA3.4/or VL-Cλ-pcDNA3.4, as described in our previous report [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref042" ref-type="bibr">42</xref>]. The antibody-expressing plasmids were co-transfected into suspension CHO-S cells (Invitrogen, USA) at a heavy-to-light chain plasmid ratio of 2:3 using the ExpiFectamin CHO Transfection Kit (Invitrogen), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Enhancer and feed components were added 16 h post-transfection. Antibody-containing supernatants were harvested 8 days after transfection. The supernatants were initially purified through Ni-chelating affinity chromatography. The concentrations of expressed mAbs were determined by measuring absorbance values at 280 nm (A280).</p></sec><sec id="sec011"><title>Indirect immunofluorescence assay</title><p>BHK-21 cells in 24-well plates were infected with O/HN/CHA/93 strain of FMDV serotype O at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1.0 for 4h at 37 °C in the presence of 5% CO<sub>2</sub>. Virus-infected cells were then fixed in precooled methanol-acetone solution at a ratio of 1:1 (v/v) for 30 min at 4 °C. After rinsing with PBS, cells were blocked for 1h at 37°C with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS. Then 200 µl per well porcine mAbs at a working concentration of 5µg/mL were added and incubated for 1h at 37°C. After washing with PBS, anti-pig IgG (whole molecule)-FITC antibody (Sigma Aldrich) at a 1:200 dilution was added and incubated in the dark for 1h at 37°C. Plates were washed three times with PBS and observed under the EVOS FL Imaging System (Life Technology, USA).</p></sec><sec id="sec012"><title>Bio-layer interferometry (BLI) assay</title><p>Prior to the BLI assay, purified O/HN/CHA/93 and O/18074 viral particles were respectively labeled with EZ-Link Sulfo-NHS-LC-LC-Biotin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and then purified using Zeba spin desalting column (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove excess non-reacted biotin. To determine the binding affinities of the porcine nAbs to FMDV, BLI measurements were performed in an Octet RED96 System according to manufacturer’s guidelines. Briefly, biotinylated O/HN/CHA/93 or O/18074 virion (10 µg/mL) was respectively immobilized onto streptavidin-coated biosensors (Pall FortéBio) until saturation. The antigen-bound biosensors were then transferred to wells containing serial dilutions of porcine nAbs to monitor the association phase, followed by immersion in dissociation buffer (0.01 M PBS supplemented with 0.1% bovine serum albumin and 0.02% Tween 20) to record dissociation kinetics. The on-rate (ka) and off-rate (kd) were determined by global fitting of the association and dissociation phases of a series of porcine nAbs concentrations. The equilibrium dissociation constant (KD), a measure of affinity, was then calculated as the ratio of kd and ka.</p></sec><sec id="sec013"><title>Virus neutralizing test</title><p>The neutralizing activities of porcine monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and porcine sera were evaluated against seven representative strains of FMDV serotype O, three representative strains of serotype A, and the rescued virus using a micro-neutralization assay as previously described [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref043" ref-type="bibr">43</xref>]. The porcine sera were obtained from four immunization groups vaccinated with inactivated vaccines containing 146S antigens derived from O/HN/CHA/93 (Cathay), O/XJ/CHA/2017 (O/Ind/2001 lineage), O/Tibet/99 (O/PanAsia lineage), or O/GSLX/2010 (O/Mya98 lineage). The FMDV serotype O panel included O/Tibet/99 and O/GZ1/2025 (ME-SA topotype); O/GSLX/2010 and O/HNNY/2022 (SEA topotype), O/HN/CHA/93 (Cathay ancient strain); and O/SCGH/CHA/2016, O/18074, O/GD/2021, O/GX/2022 (Cathay variants). The serotype A panel included A/AF72 strain (A22 lineage), A/WH/CHA/09 and A/GDMM/2013 strains (Sea97 lineage). All virus strains used in this study are listed in Table F in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>. Briefly, antibody samples were 2-fold serially diluted in 96-well cell culture plates in a total volume of 50 µl, and then 100 TCID<sub>50</sub> of FMDV in 50 µl of culture media was added to each well. After incubation for 1h at 37 °C, approximately 5 × 10<sup>4</sup> BHK-21 cells in 100 µl culture media were added to each well as indicators of residual infectivity. Normal cell wells, and virus control wells (0.1, 1, 10 and 100TCID<sub>50</sub>) in duplicate were used in each plate for comparison purpose. The plates were incubated at 37 °C under 5% CO<sub>2</sub> conditions for 72h before observing cytopathic effect (CPE). The experimental results were acceptable when complete CPE and no CPE appeared separately in 100TCID<sub>50</sub> and 0.1TCID<sub>50</sub> virus control wells. The endpoint titers were calculated as the reciprocal of the last antibody dilution to neutralize 100TCID<sub>50</sub> FMDV in 50% of the wells. Neutralizing activity was expressed as the virus neutralization (VN) titer, calculated as the initial antibody concentration divided by the endpoint dilution.</p></sec><sec id="sec014"><title>Selection of neutralization-escape mutants using porcine neutralizing antibodies</title><p>Neutralization escape mutants were generated by serial passaging of FMDV in BHK-21 cells under the selective pressure of pnAbs, following a previously described method with minor modifications [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref044" ref-type="bibr">44</xref>]. The representative FMDV strain O/HN/CHA/93 was used for mutant selection. Briefly, 10-fold serial dilutions of FMDV in 50 μl were incubated with 50 μl of various concentrations of mAbs (10 μg/mL to 20 μg/mL) in 96-well cell culture plates. The mixtures were used to infect BHK-21 cells (10<sup>6</sup> cells/mL) in a volume of 100 μl and incubated at 37˚C for 48 h to allow virus propagation. The first-passage viruses were harvested from the wells seeded with the highest dilution of virus that produced an approximately 80% to 100% cytopathic effect (CPE). Subsequent rounds of selection were performed in 24-well plates. In each round, the passaged virus (200 μl) was incubated with an equal volume of 2-fold concentration of antibodies in each well containing BHK-21 cells (400 μl). Process was repeated for multiple passages until viral replication was observed in the presence of mAbs at concentrations exceeding 400 μg/mL, indicating complete escape from antibody neutralization. For each antibody, four escape mutants (A-D) were selected using an initial mAb concentration of 10 μg/ml, and four additional mutants (E-H) were selected using 20 μg/ml. The A–D mutants were serially passaged for seven rounds up to 640 μg/ml, whereas the E–H mutants were passaged for six rounds to reach the same final concentration. Viral RNA was then extracted, and the P1 region of the escape mutants was amplified by one-step RT-PCR as previously described [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref045" ref-type="bibr">45</xref>], employing the primer pair Pan204+(ACCTCCAACGGGTGGTACGC) /NK61 (GACATGTCCTCTTGCATCTG). A portion of amplified products were verified by Sanger sequencing. Mutated amino acids were determined by aligning the entire mutant P1 region with its parent virus sequence.</p></sec><sec id="sec015"><title>Amplicon sequencing and data analysis</title><p>To quantify the mutation frequencies in the viral stocks, the remaining PCR products from parent virus and seven representative escape mutants (one per pnAb) were subjected to agarose gel electrophoresis, and the target bands were excised and purified using a gel extraction kit. The purified amplicons were then sent to GENEWIZ (Azenta Life Sciences, Suzhou, China) for amplicon sequencing on an Illumina platform. The raw sequencing data were generated as FASTQ files (PF data or Raw data). Quality control and data analysis were performed to identify mutations relative to the parental O/HN/CHA/93 sequence and to calculate the allele frequency of each variant. Reads were quality-filtered and aligned to the parental reference sequence, and variants with a frequency above the detection threshold were reported.</p></sec><sec id="sec016"><title>Rescue and titration of site-directed FMDV mutants by reverse genetics</title><p>Full-length cDNAs were generated using an established pOFS plasmid containing the complete P1 gene of FMDV strain O/HN/CHA/93. Site-directed mutagenesis was applied to introduce nucleic acid mutations to produce full-length cDNAs with single amino acid substitutions [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref046" ref-type="bibr">46</xref>]. All mutant constructs were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Recombinant FMDV mutants were rescued using a reverse genetics system as previously reported [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref004" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>]. Briefly, mutant plasmids were linearized with <italic toggle="yes">NotI</italic> and transfected into BSR/T7 cells using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The transfected cells were monitored daily for CPE appearance. At 72 h post-transfection, the culture supernatants and cells were harvested and passaged up to the fifth passage on BHK-21 cells. Viral RNA was then extracted, and the P1 region of the mutants was amplified by one-step RT-PCR, employing the primer pair Pan204+(ACCTCCAACGGGTGGTACGC) /NK61 (GACATGTCCTCTTGCATCTG). The amplified products were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Mutated amino acids were identified by aligning the entire mutant P1 region with its parent virus sequence. The fifth-passage rescued mutant viruses were measured using the plaque forming unit (PFU) assay. Confluent monolayers of BHK-21 cells were infected with 10-fold serially diluted FMDV samples in 6-well plates. Tragacanth gum (0.6%) was added after 1 h of incubation. Plaques were visualized at 48 h postinfection by fixing with acetone-methanol and staining with crystal violet. The mutant virus titers were further quantified in BHK-21 cells by calculating the 50% tissue culture infectious dose (TCID<sub>50</sub>), subsequently used to perform micro-neutralization assay as described above.</p></sec><sec id="sec017"><title>Cryo-EM sample preparation, data collection and three-dimensional reconstruction</title><p>Purified FMDV O/HN/CHA/93 146S and O/18074 146S particles were individually incubated with scFv at a molar ratio of 1:240 in a volume of 10 μl for 10–60 mins at 4˚C. A 4-μl aliquot of the mixture was applied to a glow-discharged Quantifoil grid (Au 1.2/1.3, 200 mesh). Grids were blotted for 3 s at 100% relative humidity and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher, USA). Cryo-EM data were collected on a Titan Krios G3i transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at 300 kV and equipped with a K3 BioQuantum direct electron detector (Gatan) at Lanzhou University. Micrograph images were collected as movies (15 frames, 1.5 s) and recorded at −2.0 to −0.8 μm under focus at a calibrated magnification of ×105 kX, resulting in a pixel size of 0.83 Å.</p><p>The raw movie stacks were imported into cryoSPARC [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref047" ref-type="bibr">47</xref>] for image processing and three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction. Individual frames from each micrograph movie were aligned and averaged to produce drift-corrected images. Particles were automatically picked and selected, and contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters were estimated using CTFFIND4 [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref048" ref-type="bibr">48</xref>]. Subsequent 3D reconstruction steps, including ab initio model generation, heterogeneous refinement, and homogeneous refinement, were performed in cryoSPARC. Final map resolutions were determined using the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (FSC) criterion at 0.143. The data collection and refinement statistics are summarized in Table G in <xref rid="ppat.1014650.s001" ref-type="supplementary-material">S1 Appendix</xref>.</p></sec><sec id="sec018"><title>Model building and data analysis</title><p>To construct initial atomic models of FMDV-OHN-pO18-29 and FMDV-O18-pO18-29 complexes, the cryo-EM structure of native FMDV-OTi (PDB:7D3K) [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref015" ref-type="bibr">15</xref>] and the AlphaFold2-predicted structure of pO18-29 [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref049" ref-type="bibr">49</xref>] were manually placed into the corresponding cryo-EM density maps and rigid-body fitted with UCSF Chimera [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref050" ref-type="bibr">50</xref>]. The resulting complex models were subsequently refined by real-space refinement in Phenix [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref051" ref-type="bibr">51</xref>]. Manual model building was performed using Coot [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref052" ref-type="bibr">52</xref>], followed by additional rounds of real-space refinement in Phenix to improve the agreement between the models and the density maps. The final models were validated using MolProbity [<xref rid="ppat.1014650.ref053" ref-type="bibr">53</xref>].</p></sec></sec><sec id="sec019" sec-type="supplementary-material"><title>Supporting information</title><supplementary-material id="ppat.1014650.s001" position="float" content-type="local-data" orientation="portrait"><label>S1 Appendix</label><caption><title>Suppementary figures and tables.</title><p>(DOCX)</p></caption><media xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="ppat.1014650.s001.docx" position="float" orientation="portrait"><?suppdata-name ppat.1014650.s001.docx?><?suppdata-size 17901463?><?suppdata-md5 8c2b84237d6afdc23924ac8fdf469148?><?suppdata-image-server-status NEVER_LOAD?><?suppdata-mime-type application?><?suppdata-mime-sub-type vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document?><?suppdata-cloudpmc-urn urn:app:7418/13671523/8c2b84237d6a/ppat.1014650.s001.docx?></media></supplementary-material></sec></body><back><ack><p>We thank the Supercomputing Center of Lanzhou University for providing facilities.
