</p><p>Structural basis of antigenic drift in FMDV O/Cathay topotype variants revealed by porcine-derived single B-cell neutralizing antibodies</p><p>PLOS Pathogens</p><p>Dear Dr. Li,</p><p>Thank you for submitting your manuscript to PLOS Pathogens. After careful consideration, we feel that it has merit but does not fully meet PLOS Pathogens's publication criteria as it currently stands. Therefore, we invite you to submit a revised version of the manuscript that addresses the points raised during the review process.</p><p>Please submit your revised manuscript by September 30. If you will need more time than this to complete your revisions, please reply to this message or contact the journal office at <email>plospathogens@plos.org</email>. When you're ready to submit your revision, log on to <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://www.editorialmanager.com/ppathogens/" ext-link-type="uri">https://www.editorialmanager.com/ppathogens/</ext-link> and select the 'Submissions Needing Revision' folder to locate your manuscript file.</p><p>Please include the following items when submitting your revised manuscript:</p><p>* A letter that responds to each point raised by the editor and reviewer(s). You should upload this letter as a separate file labeled 'Response to Reviewers'. This file does not need to include responses to any formatting updates and technical items listed in the 'Journal Requirements' section below.</p><p>* A marked-up copy of your manuscript that highlights changes made to the original version. You should upload this as a separate file labeled 'Revised Manuscript with Track Changes'.</p><p>* An unmarked version of your revised paper without tracked changes. You should upload this as a separate file labeled 'Manuscript'.</p><p>We look forward to receiving your revised manuscript.</p><p>Kind regards,</p><p>Margarita Saiz, Ph.D.</p><p>Academic Editor</p><p>PLOS Pathogens</p><p>Sonja Best</p><p>Section Editor</p><p>Editor-in-Chief</p><p>PLOS Pathogens</p><p>orcid.org/0000-0003-2946-9497</p><p>Michael Malim</p><p>Editor-in-Chief</p><p>PLOS Pathogens</p><p>orcid.org/0000-0002-7699-2064</p><p>
<bold>Additional Editor Comments (if provided):</bold>
</p><p>Dear Dr Li,</p><p>Your manuscript has been revised by three experts in the field. Please find their comments at the end of this message. They all agree on the interest and relevance of the work. However, a significant number of concerns have been raised that need to be addressed. The draft should be deeply revised for clarity and correction according to their comments. I´ll be willing to consider a revised manuscript for publication in PLOS Pathogens.</p><p>
<bold>Journal Requirements:</bold>
</p><p>If the reviewer comments include a recommendation to cite specific previously published works, please review and evaluate these publications to determine whether they are relevant and should be cited. There is no requirement to cite these works unless the editor has indicated otherwise.</p><p>1) Thank you for stating "The cryo-EM density maps and structures for FMDV-OHN-pO18-29 and FMDV-O18-pO18-29 have been deposited into the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) with the following accession numbers: FMDV-OHN-pO18-29, EMD-69003, PDB 23IT, and FMDV-O18-pO18-29, EMD-69004, PDB 23IU." However, we were unable to access the accession number using the information provided. Please review and update the Data Availability Statement to ensure that the underlying data are publicly accessible and that all accession numbers, links, or repository details are correct and functional.</p><p>2) We have amended your Competing Interest statement to comply with journal style. We kindly ask that you double check the statement and let us know if anything is incorrect.</p><p>
<bold>Reviewers' Comments:</bold>
</p><p>Reviewer's Responses to Questions</p><p>
<bold>Part I - Summary</bold>
</p><p>Please use this section to discuss strengths/weaknesses of study, novelty/significance, general execution and scholarship.</p><p>Reviewer #1: The manuscript presents a well-executed study on antigenic drift in FMDV topotype variants using porcine-derived single B cell neutralizing antibodies. The study is methodologically solid, combining reverse genetics, scFv production, and cryo-electron microscopy to characterize antibody–virus interactions. The work is relevant for understanding antigenic variability and its implications for immune escape and vaccine design in swine populations. Overall, the results are convincing, and the main novelty lies in the functional and structural validation of antigenic determinants in infectious virus systems.</p><p>Reviewer #2: Li et al., have used a panel of seven porcine-derived neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (pnAbs) to identify antigenic regions responsible for neutralization escape from porcine immune sera in recent FMDV O/Cathay variants. A charge modification at +2 residue (Q→H/R) downstream the conserved RGD receptor-binding motif on VP1 (within a region well characterized as a relevant B cell antigenic site), modulates sensitivity to different pnAbs and vaccine-induced sera. In addition, cryo-EM structures of one of the pnAbs (pO18-29) in complex with the ancient O/HN/CHA/93 strain (the strain used as a reference in this study) and the recent variant O/18074 revealed a novel conformation-dependent, VP3-centered antigen determinant. Substitutions leading to charge modifications at positions 73 and 134 on VP3 disrupt hydrophobic contacts, hydrogen bonds, and salt bridges, leading the virus to escape different antibodies. Interestingly, these two VP3 residues act cooperatively to regulate antibody recognition.</p><p>The authors conclude that the results contribute to elucidate the structural basis of neutralizing evasion in O/Cathay and support the rational design of next-generation broad-spectrum FMDV vaccine against emerging O/Cathay variants.</p><p>General comments</p><p>The topic of this manuscript is interesting as O/Cathay topotype has accumulated mutations over time associated with antigenic drift that can become a real problem in terms of vaccine effectiveness in different Asian regions. In general, this manuscript is well written and describes a comprehensive and, in my opinion, well conducted original work. Porcine-derived neutralizing mAbs are also interesting and suited tools for the analysis of the antigenic structures recognized by pig sera.</p><p>Nevertheless, there are issues regarding data and manuscript presentation as well as discussion that have to be addressed. In this line, the interesting statement at the end of the Abstract “Together, our findings elucidate ….. and provide a molecular framework for rational design of next-generation broad-spectrum FMDV vaccine …… “deserves further attention. The authors can discuss in more detail how these kinds of results can be translated into vaccine optimization and matching, as well as their potential impact on conventional as well as subunit vaccines.</p><p>In addition, a comparison of the genetic distances among the type O viruses analyzed, such as a P1 phylogenetic tree, will be valuable to determine correlations between genetic drift (nucleotide substitutions) and the antigenic changes among the O/Cathay variants. The inclusion of such comparison will improve the analyses of the data presented.</p><p>Reviewer #3: It has been reported that newly emerging FMDV O/Cathay strains circulating in China can escape neutralization by sera from vaccinated pigs due to the accumulation of mutations that reduce antibody-mediated neutralization and compromise vaccine efficacy. In this manuscript, the authors investigate recently emerged O/Cathay variants that exhibit this immune escape phenotype. The main strength and novelty of the study lies in the structural characterization of the molecular determinants underlying antigenic divergence through the combined use of cryo-electron microscopy and porcine neutralizing monoclonal antibodies.</p><p>The authors identify two key antigenic regions involved in immune escape: one located adjacent to the RGD motif in VP1 and a second, previously unrecognized, region in VP3. They demonstrate that two point mutations affecting VP3 disrupt critical molecular interactions and act cooperatively to confer resistance to antibody-mediated neutralization.</p><p>The methodology used is appropriate for the study’s objectives and is described in sufficient detail. However, the use of unpaired t-tests with Holm–Šidák correction is not statistically appropriate for this experimental design, which compares vaccine-induced neutralizing antibody titers against the homologous virus and four viral variants. A more appropriate approach would be a one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s multiple-comparison test if the objective is to compare each viral variant exclusively with the homologous virus, or Tukey’s multiple-comparison test if all pairwise comparisons among variants are intended.</p><p>Recent outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease in China have also been caused by two additional serotype O topotypes, Middle East–South Asia (ME-SA) and Southeast Asia (SEA). Is it known whether these topotypes, like Cathay, also exhibit escape from vaccine-induced neutralization? If so, are these escape phenotypes associated with the same mutations and structural alterations identified in the present study? Otherwise, to what extent can the conclusions of this manuscript be generalized to other serotype O topotypes?</p><p>Overall, the study is scientifically relevant and provides valuable structural insights into the mechanisms by which emerging FMDV variants evade vaccine-induced immune responses. These findings improve our understanding of the antigenic evolution of the O/Cathay topotype and provide a rational framework for the design of next-generation vaccines with broader cross-protective efficacy against antigenically divergent strains.</p><p>**********</p><p>

</p><p>Please use this section to detail the key new experiments or modifications of existing experiments that should be <underline>absolutely</underline> required to validate study conclusions.</p><p>Generally, there should be no more than 3 such required experiments or major modifications for a "Major Revision" recommendation. Although viral antigenic evolution is shaped by the competing demands of immune evasion and receptor-binding fitness, the physical principles underlying divergent viral evolutionary dynamics remain poorly understood. Here, by integrating structural biology, deep mutational scanning, and genomic surveillance data, we show that receptor-binding geometry constrains the spatial coupling between antibody escape and intrinsic viral fitness. In SARS-CoV-2, the exposed convex Spike-ACE2 interface spatially overlaps dominant neutralizing epitopes with receptor-contact residues, producing a stringent fitness-evasion trade-off. Consequently, viable escape mutations are largely restricted to a narrow peripheral region surrounding the receptor-binding core. As population immunity progressively saturates this limited escape space, continued adaptation increasingly requires coordinated saltational remodeling of the receptor-binding interface. In contrast, the influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin binds the small sialic acid ligand through a recessed pocket architecture that partially separates dominant antibody pressure from receptor-binding fitness constraints. This topological decoupling permits continuous stepwise antigenic drift without requiring frequent remodeling of the core binding site. Building on these findings, we develop a lightweight geometry-based framework that accurately identifies receptor-competitive antigenic hotspots across divergent viruses. Together, our results support a general model in which receptor geometry and protein surface topology strongly bias accessible antigenic evolutionary trajectories.

IMPORTANCE

Why some viruses evolve through gradual antigenic drift whereas others undergo recurrent evolutionary leaps remains a fundamental question in virology. By integrating protein structures, mutational scanning data, and genomic surveillance, we show that the geometry of the receptor-binding interface strongly influences how immune escape mutations affect viral fitness. In SARS-CoV-2, receptor-binding residues are highly exposed and overlap with dominant antibody targets, restricting immune escape to a narrow set of mutations and promoting periodic evolutionary leaps when this space becomes exhausted. In contrast, the receptor-binding pocket of influenza A virus H3N2 is partially shielded from antibody recognition, allowing continuous antigenic drift with fewer fitness constraints. We further demonstrate that these structural principles can be used to identify antigenic hotspots directly from virus-receptor complexes. These findings provide a mechanistic explanation for divergent viral evolutionary trajectories and offer a structural framework for studying and anticipating antigenic evolution.

KEYWORDS: antigenic evolution, phylodynamics, H3N2, SARS-CoV-2

INTRODUCTION

The evolutionary dynamics of human viruses are shaped by a fundamental tension between immune evasion and the maintenance of transmissibility (1). Mutations that alter antigenic surfaces can reduce antibody recognition, yet these same mutations often compromise viral intrinsic fitness such as receptor binding and cell entry. Although this trade-off represents a common selective pressure across many viruses, different pathogens exhibit remarkably distinct phylodynamic behaviors (2). SARS-CoV-2 has undergone recurrent lineage replacement and punctuated genetic turnover throughout the pandemic (3), whereas influenza H3N2 typically evolves through comparatively gradual and continuous antigenic drift (4, 5). The biophysical principles underlying these divergent evolutionary trajectories remain poorly understood.

Substantial efforts have therefore been devoted to characterizing and predicting viral antigenic evolution through approaches including deep mutational scanning (DMS), phylogenetic inference, and machine learning models (6–8). These studies have collectively revealed that many viral proteins possess a surprisingly large theoretical landscape of escape mutations. However, integrating these experimental landscapes with global genomic surveillance data reveals a striking discrepancy. Although numerous mutations exhibit strong immune escape potential in vitro, only a limited subset repeatedly emerges and successfully spreads in natural populations (1, 9), suggesting that the majority of theoretically immune escape mutations remain evolutionarily inaccessible under real-world selective constraints.

A prevailing explanation for this discrepancy is the severe fitness cost associated with altering the receptor-binding interface. Because the most potent neutralizing antibodies frequently target surfaces involved in host receptor engagement, immune escape mutations often impair viral entry efficiency or transmissibility (10–12). Previous studies have emphasized the role of epistasis in alleviating this constraint, suggesting that compensatory mutations alter the global fitness landscape to make otherwise deleterious escape mutations tolerable (13–15). Alternatively, the virus may adopt a stepwise, “Z-shaped” evolutionary trajectory by promoting its transmissibility first and then trading it for enhanced immune evasion (1). While these models successfully explain specific lineage dynamics, they do not fully address why distinct viruses experience markedly different degrees of fitness-evasion conflict in the first place.

One possible explanation is that structural features of viral receptor-binding proteins influence how immune escape mutations affect receptor engagement (8, 16, 17). Because receptor-binding interfaces vary substantially in their geometry and exposure, different viruses may experience distinct constraints on the accessibility of antigenic mutations. However, whether receptor-binding architecture systematically shapes antigenic evolution remains unclear. In particular, it is unknown whether the pronounced fitness-evasion trade-offs observed in SARS-CoV-2 reflect a general feature of viral evolution or arise from specific structural properties of its receptor-binding interface.

In this study, we integrate high-resolution structural biology, DMS-derived functional measurements, and large-scale genomic surveillance data to investigate how receptor-binding geometry shapes viral antigenic evolution. Through comparative analyses of the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein and the influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin (HA), we demonstrate that protein surface topology strongly influences the spatial coupling between antibody escape and receptor-binding fitness. These geometric constraints define distinct accessible evolutionary modes and help explain the contrasting phylodynamic behaviors of SARS-CoV-2 and H3N2. Building on this mechanistic framework, we further develop a lightweight geometry-based computational approach that identifies receptor-competitive antigenic hotspots directly from virus-receptor structures, providing an interpretable structural framework for studying viral antigenic evolution.

RESULTSReceptor-binding geometry spatially couples antibody escape with receptor fitness in SARS-CoV-2

To investigate how structural topology constrains SARS-CoV-2 antigenic evolution, we first projected the Spike protein structure into a two-dimensional (2D) spatial representation using multidimensional scaling (MDS), assigning each amino acid residue a representative coordinate derived from the three-dimensional (3D) PDB structure. As shown in Fig. 1A, the resulting projection recapitulated the overall side-view architecture of a Spike protomer, with the receptor-binding domain (RBD) positioned at the top and the N-terminal domain (NTD) on the right.

Each data point represents an individual amino acid residue, with shapes indicating distinct structural domains. We then mapped the weighted contact number (WCN), a proxy for local structural packing and solvent exposure, onto this projection. Regions on the outer periphery of both the RBD and NTD exhibited low WCN values, indicating high surface accessibility to antibody recognition (Fig. 1A) (18). Overlaying site-specific human ACE2 (hACE2) binding impact (transformed from mutation-level DMS measurements, representing the normalized absolute mutational impact per site; see Materials and Methods) revealed that residues most critical for receptor engagement clustered within the exposed RBD interface and similarly exhibited low WCN values (Fig. 1B). Several distal regions, such as the stalk, also exhibited a moderate impact on ACE2 binding, likely by altering the conformation of the Spike trimer (e.g., shifting the RBD states) (11, 19).

Based on conventional antigenic drift models, highly exposed regions that minimally disrupt receptor binding are expected to represent optimal evolutionary targets for immune escape (18, 20, 21). By this logic, the NTD should provide a favorable mutational landscape because it is strongly exposed yet largely dispensable for direct ACE2 engagement. However, pseudovirus-assay DMS serum escape profiles (11) revealed a markedly different pattern. Rather than broadly distributing across all exposed surfaces, site-specific serum escape impact closely mirrored the spatial footprint of ACE2 binding (Fig. 1C). The highly exposed residues of the NTD contributed relatively little to serum escape, whereas the dominant escape hotspots localized overwhelmingly within the RBD. Consistent with this observation, mutations that strongly enhanced serum escape generally impaired receptor binding. Across both KP.3.1.1 and XBB.1.5 data sets (11), mutation-level ACE2-binding scores exhibited a strong negative correlation with mutation-level serum escape scores (Fig. 1D), indicating that immune evasion and receptor engagement are intrinsically coupled within the Spike RBD.

This phenomenon, where the most potent escape mutations cluster within the RBD, was noted in the original DMS studies (11). However, due to the polyclonal nature of immune sera, it remained unclear whether this clustering occurs because the human humoral response is preferentially directed toward the RBD, or because only antibodies targeting the receptor-binding interface efficiently neutralize the virus. To distinguish between these possibilities, we incorporated an independent yeast-display DMS data set profiling individual serum antibodies and their corresponding neutralization activities (22, 23).

Analysis of the antibody profiles demonstrated that antibodies were generated broadly against nearly the entire exposed surface (Fig. S1). However, antibodies targeting residues proximal to the receptor-binding interface exhibited substantially greater neutralization potency than antibodies targeting more distal regions (Fig. 1E). Thus, although antibodies recognize diverse exposed epitopes, the most effective antibodies are those that sterically compete with receptor engagement (12).

After recognizing that steric competition, rather than mere solvent exposure, determines the functional importance of antibody escape, one might expect the strongest escape mutations to cluster directly on the absolute core of the receptor-binding interface. However, as observed in Fig. 1C, the most potent escape sites within the RBD are situated adjacent to, rather than precisely within, the core contact interface. Correspondingly, the correlation between mutation-level ACE2 binding scores and mutation-level serum escape scores was weaker in the RBD than in other regions of the Spike. This is likely because mutations in non-RBD regions can alter the conformational equilibrium of the Spike trimer, thereby simultaneously impacting receptor accessibility and the exposure of neutralizing epitopes (10, 11, 24), and also suggests the existence of a local spatial conflict in the RBD between optimal immune escape and maximal receptor binding (Fig. S2).

To unravel this spatial discrepancy, we examined the relationship between serum escape and several structural features. Among all tested variables, the physical distance to the receptor exhibits a significant but remarkably divergent correlation depending on the spatial scales examined (Fig. 1F). Globally across the Spike protein, residues located closer to the receptor generally displayed stronger immune escape potential. However, within the RBD itself, this trend reversed. Mapping serum escape impact scores as a function of receptor distance revealed that residue escape potential increased progressively when approaching the binding interface from distal regions, but peaked within a peripheral region approximately 25–40 Å from the interface before declining near the receptor-contact surface (Fig. 1G).

We hypothesized that this reduction in escape impact at the immediate receptor-contact surface reflects receptor fitness constraints imposed by the pseudovirus assay. Because productive infection requires sufficient receptor engagement and cell entry, mutations that excessively disrupt ACE2 binding cannot generate detectable escape signals even if they strongly perturb antibody recognition (10). Therefore, the receptor-contact core represents a region of maximal steric competitiveness but minimal mutational tolerance. To validate this hypothesis, we analyzed the site-specific escape impact scores derived from the yeast-display assay, which quantify neutralization-weighted antibody recognition independently of receptor fitness (hereafter referred to as antibody escape impact). In contrast to pseudovirus serum escape impact scores, antibody escape impact increased monotonically as residues approached the receptor interface, without exhibiting a peripheral turning point (Fig. 1H; Fig. S3). The strongest geometric escape sites are precisely those on the direct receptor-contact surface.

Together, these findings demonstrate that the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein exhibits a tightly coupled fitness-evasion architecture. The exposed convex Spike-ACE2 interface spatially overlaps dominant neutralizing epitopes with essential receptor-contact residues, generating a constrained evolutionary landscape in which viable escape mutations are largely restricted to a narrow peripheral region surrounding the receptor-binding core.

Spatial fitness constraints restrict accessible antigenic evolutionary pathways in SARS-CoV-2

Given that the preceding analysis was derived primarily from in vitro experimental data, it is important to verify whether these spatial fitness constraints govern the real-world antigenic evolutionary dynamics of SARS-CoV-2. To specifically examine mutations likely driven by immune selection rather than stochastic drift or direct transmissibility enhancement, we focused on mutations exhibiting measurable immune escape together with reduced ACE2-binding affinity.

As shown in Fig. 2A, the spatial distribution of escape mutation incidence (independent occurrence events on the phylogenetic tree, representing short-term evolutionary dynamics) differs markedly from the landscape of site-specific yeast-display antibody escape impact scores. Instead, it closely resembles the constrained pseudovirus serum escape profile. Although the receptor-contact core (0–5 Å) exhibited the highest theoretical steric competitiveness, the highest density of naturally occurring escape mutations concentrated within a narrow annular region located approximately 5–10 Å from the receptor interface. This spatial preference was consistently observed across all major clades (Fig. S4), suggesting that the enrichment was unlikely to result from lineage-specific antibody targeting biases (12).

These evolutionary hotspots correspond to an annular region immediately surrounding the receptor-contact core (Fig. 2B). Consistent with the fitness-evasion trade-off observed in Fig. 1, residues within this peripheral region exert a substantially weaker impact on ACE2 binding than direct contact residues (Fig. 2C), suggesting that it represents the most evolutionarily accessible region for receptor-competitive immune escape.

Interestingly, this optimal evolutionary region observed in real-world viral evolution was substantially closer to the receptor interface than the peak escape region inferred from pseudovirus assays (25–40 Å; Fig. 1G). This spatial shift suggests that naturally evolving viral populations can tolerate greater receptor-binding perturbations than artificial mutants measured experimentally, probably because epistatic interactions and combinatorial mutations partially compensate for local fitness costs, or result from dynamic selection pressures (25).

To determine whether the threshold of acceptable receptor-binding perturbations shifted over time during viral evolution, we compared mutation-level ACE2-binding profiles across multiple SARS-CoV-2 clades. While BA.5 and XBB.1.5 exhibited substantially elevated baseline ACE2-binding affinities compared to the Wild-type or early Omicron variants (Fig. 2D), this increase did not expand the viable mutational landscape. Rather, mutations that successfully emerged also exhibited proportionally higher binding scores. These observations indicate that the fitness threshold is not fixed, but dynamically determined by the competitive epidemiological environment and the evolving population immunity landscape (26).

The observation that short-term escape evolution preferentially targets the peripheral interface raises an important evolutionary question: if the receptor-contact core is sub-optimal for evasion, why is it not evolutionarily conserved? Long-term evolutionary rate analyses revealed that the receptor-contact surface (0–5 Å) actually accumulates amino acid mutations at the highest rate across the pandemic, doubling the rate observed within the 5–10 Å periphery (Fig. 2E; Fig. S5). To resolve this discrepancy, we separated SARS-CoV-2 evolution into two distinct modes: continuous stepwise evolution and saltational lineage transition (evolutionary leap). During stepwise evolution, mutation events were strongly enriched within the peripheral 5–10 Å region, consistent with the fitness-constrained escape landscape described above. In contrast, major saltational lineage transitions preferentially introduced mutations directly within the receptor-contact core (Fig. 2F). Thus, the elevated long-term evolutionary rate of the core interface is largely driven by evolutionary leaps rather than antigenic drift.

Together, these findings suggest that the exposed Spike-ACE2 geometry imposes a progressively narrowing evolutionary landscape on SARS-CoV-2. During routine circulation, immune escape proceeds primarily through peripheral receptor-competitive mutations that partially preserve receptor engagement. However, as repeated exposure and immune imprinting saturate this limited mutational space, continued antigenic adaptation increasingly requires coordinated saltational remodeling of the receptor-binding interface itself.

Receptor-binding topology determines distinct antigenic evolutionary modes across viruses

To determine whether the spatial coupling between viral immune escape and receptor fitness observed in SARS-CoV-2 represents a universal property of viral evolution or a consequence of its specific receptor-binding architecture, we next examined influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin (HA), which exhibits a markedly different phylodynamic pattern characterized by more continuous stepwise antigenic drift. Unlike SARS-CoV-2, which engages a large proteinaceous receptor (hACE2), H3N2 utilizes the HA protein to bind sialic acid (SIA), a low-molecular-weight glycan, to mediate host cell entry (27).

This difference in receptor size produces a distinct binding topology. Whereas the Spike RBD forms an exposed convex receptor-binding surface, the HA receptor-binding site consists of a recessed concave pocket that accommodates the small SIA ligand (Fig. 3A). This concave architecture largely allows HA to maintain receptor binding through the collective structural integrity of the pocket rather than relying on a limited set of surface-exposed residues (16). Consequently, the two viruses exhibit distinct constraints regarding mutational viability in pseudovirus-based assays. In the pseudovirus DMS profile (28), H3N2 core mutations (0–5 Å) yielded detectable serum escape signals even when incurring severe cell entry penalties (Fig. 3B). Conversely, analogous core mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD greatly disrupted receptor engagement, frequently compromised pseudovirus viability (Fig. S6A), and obstructed accurate escape measurement (Fig. 1G; Fig. S6B).

Thus, the distinct topology of the HA receptor-binding pocket dramatically altered the viable spatial landscape of immune escape (29). Unlike SARS-CoV-2, the site-specific H3N2 pseudovirus-assay serum escape impact scores continue to rise as residues approach the contact surface (Fig. 3C). However, the pocket structure physically inverted the antigenic significance of receptor proximity. Relative solvent accessibility (RSA) and WCN indices both indicate that residues in the immediate contact region (0–5 Å) were largely buried within the pocket architecture (Fig. 3C and D). Thus, although these core residues possess strong theoretical steric competitiveness, they are likely shielded from direct antibody accessibility (30, 31). The high in vitro escape scores observed within the buried core likely arise indirectly through allosteric conformational effects (28). Importantly, mutations within the core pocket also imposed significantly greater fitness costs than peripheral mutations (Fig. 3E), further limiting their evolutionary accessibility.

The real-world genomic surveillance strongly supported this structural interpretation. Genomic surveillance data demonstrated that naturally circulating H3N2 strains preferentially accumulated escape-associated mutations within the exposed rim surrounding the receptor-binding pocket rather than within the buried receptor-contact core (Fig. 3F) (32). Correspondingly, residues in this peripheral region also accumulated substitutions at substantially higher long-term evolutionary rates than direct receptor-contact residues (Fig. 3G; Fig. S7). Thus, although the pocket core remains important for receptor binding, it contributes relatively little to long-term antigenic turnover.

This evolutionary pattern differs from that observed in SARS-CoV-2. In SARS-CoV-2, the exposed ACE2-binding surface forces receptor engagement and dominant neutralizing epitopes to occupy the same spatial region, creating a progressively constrained evolutionary landscape in which continued adaptation ultimately requires remodeling of the receptor-contact core. In contrast, the recessed HA pocket shifts much of the antigenically accessible surface away from the receptor-contact residues. Consequently, H3N2 can achieve substantial antigenic diversification through mutations surrounding the pocket while largely preserving the structurally constrained core.

Together, these findings reveal that receptor geometry and interface topology fundamentally reshape the spatial coupling between viral immune escape and receptor-binding fitness, which eventually constrains viral antigenic evolution trajectories.

Modeling steric competitiveness enables prediction of receptor-competitive antigenic hotspots

Because our analyses consistently identified steric competition at the receptor interface as the dominant structural determinant of immune escape, we next asked whether these geometric constraints could be directly leveraged to predict antigenic sites.

Thus, we developed a lightweight structure-based computational framework to quantify receptor competitiveness of individual residues directly from virus-receptor complex structures. For each residue, a virtual spherical probe representing the approximate steric bulk of a neutralizing antibody was positioned on the solvent-accessible surface (or centered at the alpha carbon) (Fig. 4A). We then quantified the number of receptor atoms intersecting this sphere, defining the resulting value as the receptor clash number. To account for baseline physical accessibility, the clash number was multiplied by the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) index and normalized, generating a final site competitiveness score. Conceptually, this metric estimates the extent to which antibody binding at a given residue would sterically interfere with receptor engagement. Highly competitive sites therefore represent structurally accessible regions capable of directly disrupting receptor binding through antibody occupancy.

Applying this framework to the SARS-CoV-2 Spike and H3N2 HA proteins, we found that high competitiveness values were predominantly localized to the receptor-binding periphery, while distal sites exhibited minimal competitiveness due to the absence of receptor overlap (Fig. 4B and C). Importantly, site competitiveness strongly correlated with site-specific DMS escape impact scores across both viruses (Fig. 4D and E). Furthermore, competitiveness values also correlated significantly with real-world mutation incidence (Fig. 4F), indicating that receptor competitiveness acts as a major determinant of antigenic evolution.

We next benchmarked our geometry-based framework against EVEscape, a machine learning framework that predicts viral escape potential from sequence evolution and functional constraint patterns (33). Strikingly, our lightweight structural algorithm outperformed EVEscape in predicting DMS escape scores (Spearman correlation = 0.31 vs 0.29 for SARS-CoV-2; 0.19 vs −0.065 for H3N2, Fig. S8 and S9). While EVEscape effectively captures whether mutations are evolutionarily permissible, it does not explicitly model the geometry-dependent coupling between antibody escape and receptor binding revealed in this study. By multiplying our competitiveness values with EVEscape predictions, we achieved a model that enables full-protein prediction with substantially improved accuracy (Fig. S10), suggesting that receptor competitiveness represents an orthogonal and previously underweighted structural feature in existing predictive models.

We next investigated whether receptor-binding topology itself is evolutionarily conserved enough to permit cross-species structural prediction, an important scenario for anticipating the evolutionary trajectories of newly emerging viruses prior to the experimental resolution of their native structures. To test this possibility, we chose SARS-related coronavirus (SARS-CoV) and 2009 pandemic influenza A virus (H1N1pdm09) as predictive surrogates for SARS-CoV-2 and H3N2, respectively (34, 35).

Despite significant divergence in their amino acid sequences and distinct antigenic profiles, the estimated competitiveness footprints aligned significantly well between structurally related pairs (Fig. 4G and H). The competitiveness profiles of SARS-CoV/SARS-CoV-2 (both binding hACE2), as well as H1N1pdm09/H3N2 (both binding SIA), exhibited highly similar competitiveness landscapes. Crucially, the competitiveness scores derived from these surrogate structures remained highly predictive of the DMS escape profiles of their counterparts (Fig. S11).

To further test our model across truly divergent viruses utilizing the same receptor, we used the structure of influenza B (Yamagata lineage; PDB: 2RFU) as a surrogate to predict the antigenic evolutionary landscape of influenza A H3N2. Despite their distant evolutionary relationship, the competitiveness profile derived from influenza B significantly predicted the H3N2 DMS escape profile (Fig. S12).

Collectively, these results establish steric receptor competitiveness as a fundamental structural determinant of viral antigenic evolution. Although viruses can diversify extensively at the sequence level, they remain constrained by the underlying geometric architecture required for receptor engagement. In a sense, host receptor geometry itself provides a structural blueprint for identifying receptor-competitive antigenic hotspots and anticipating accessible evolutionary trajectories across diverse viral systems.

DISCUSSION

In this study, we integrated structural biophysics, DMS data sets, and global genomic surveillance to investigate how receptor-binding geometry constrains viral antigenic evolution. Our analyses support a general framework in which the spatial relationship between receptor engagement and antibody accessibility strongly shapes the evolutionary pathways available to a virus. Specifically, we show that potent neutralizing escape mutations preferentially arise at receptor-competitive sites, where antibody binding sterically interferes with host receptor engagement. However, because these same regions are often required for efficient viral entry, immune escape is intrinsically constrained by the need to preserve receptor fitness.

Our results suggest that the strength of this fitness-evasion coupling is not universal, but instead depends heavily on the geometric organization of the receptor-binding interface. In influenza H3N2, the HA protein engages the small SIA ligand through a recessed binding pocket. This concave architecture allows receptor recognition to rely on the collective structural integrity of the pocket rather than a highly exposed receptor-contact surface. As a consequence, many receptor-contacting residues remain relatively shielded from direct antibody accessibility, partially separating receptor-binding fitness from dominant neutralizing pressure (16). This topological organization expands the range of antigenically accessible yet fitness-tolerable mutations, enabling the gradual and continuous antigenic drift characteristic of H3N2 evolution.

In contrast, the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein engages a large proteinaceous receptor, hACE2, through an exposed convex interface (36). Under this geometry, receptor-contact residues and dominant neutralizing epitopes become spatially superimposed. Consequently, mutations that strongly disrupt antibody recognition frequently impair receptor engagement simultaneously, producing a substantially tighter fitness-evasion trade-off. Our analyses indicate that the viable evolutionary space is therefore concentrated within a narrow peripheral region surrounding the absolute receptor-contact surface, where mutations can partially disrupt antibody competition while preserving sufficient ACE2-binding affinity (Fig. S13). Notably, even variants with substantially enhanced baseline ACE2-binding affinity did not exhibit a proportional expansion of accessible mutational space, suggesting that viral fitness is context-dependent rather than absolute (14). In highly competitive epidemiological environments, even modest reductions in receptor engagement may impose substantial selective disadvantages (25).

These spatial constraints may also help explain the unusual long-term evolutionary dynamics of SARS-CoV-2. Early in population immunity development, escape mutations within the peripheral receptor-competitive region can effectively reduce neutralization while maintaining transmissibility (12). However, repeated infections and vaccinations progressively reshape the antibody landscape through immunological imprinting, concentrating humoral responses toward previously encountered and relatively conserved epitopes (37, 38). As the accessible peripheral escape space becomes increasingly saturated, the virus faces growing pressure to alter residues closer to the receptor-binding core. Because isolated escape mutations within this region often impose severe fitness costs, successful adaptation may require coordinated combinations of compensatory mutations capable of traversing otherwise inaccessible fitness valleys. This framework provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for the “evolutionary leaps” of SARS-CoV-2, which often involve complex epistatic networks that globally alter the fitness landscape (13, 15, 39).

At the same time, our findings do not imply that receptor geometry alone determines viral evolution. Multiple additional processes, including epistasis, transmission ecology, host population immunity, glycan shielding, and stochastic epidemiological dynamics (3, 40–42), also shape evolutionary outcomes. Rather, our results suggest that receptor-binding topology constitutes an important physical constraint that strongly biases which evolutionary trajectories remain accessible under immune selection. In this context, the contrasting behaviors of SARS-CoV-2 and H3N2 may reflect different degrees of spatial coupling between neutralization pressure and receptor fitness, rather than fundamentally distinct evolutionary principles.

Building on this mechanistic framework, we developed a lightweight structural metric termed “site competitiveness” to estimate the potential for steric competition between antibody binding and receptor engagement directly from virus-receptor complex structures. Despite its simplicity, this geometry-based framework showed significant predictive power for experimentally measured escape scores and real-world mutation incidence across divergent viral systems. Notably, competitiveness landscapes remained highly conserved between structurally related viruses sharing the same receptor usage, even when their amino acid sequences and antigenic properties differed substantially. These observations suggest that receptor-binding geometry may impose conserved topological constraints that persist across evolutionary divergence.

Several limitations should nevertheless be acknowledged. First, our framework primarily captures receptor-competitive neutralization and may underrepresent other immune escape mechanisms such as conformational effects, complement activation, or Fc-mediated effector functions (11, 43, 44). Similarly, cellular immunity imposes selective pressures that are mechanistically distinct from steric inhibition of receptor engagement and are therefore not explicitly modeled here (45). Furthermore, although our “site competitiveness” framework relies on a physical approximation of antibody dimensions, real-world antibody-antigen interactions exhibit substantial structural and chemical diversity that is not considered within this geometric abstraction.

Second, our comparative analyses focused mainly on SARS-CoV-2 and influenza H3N2 because comprehensive DMS data sets and high-resolution receptor-bound structures remain unavailable for many human viruses. Additional viral data sets will be required to determine how broadly these geometric principles generalize across diverse receptor architectures and entry mechanisms. For instance, while SARS-CoV-2 and HCoV-NL63 both utilize the ACE2 protein receptor, they belong to different coronavirus genera and exhibit distinct Spike topologies (46). Conversely, HCoV-OC43 binds small sialic acid (SIA) ligands, a receptor class typically associated with influenza viruses (47); thus, its immune escape landscape likely mirrors influenza more closely than its coronavirus relatives (2).

Even more intriguingly, while conventional influenza A viruses utilize small SIA receptors, the H2N2 and bat-derived H17N10 and H18N11 have evolved to utilize the bulky host MHC-II protein for cellular entry (48–50). According to our geometric framework, we would hypothesize that the HA proteins of those viruses, driven by the steric constraints of a large proteinaceous receptor, should exhibit a highly constrained, SARS-CoV-2-like evolutionary landscape, distinct from the broad mutational tolerance observed in SIA-binding H3N2.

Finally, our computational framework relies strictly on a priori knowledge of the virus-receptor complex. For emerging novel viruses, precisely identifying the correct entry receptor remains a significant challenge, even with advanced machine learning tools (51, 52).

Overall, our study supports a model in which receptor geometry and protein surface topology strongly influence how immune pressure and receptor fitness are spatially coupled during viral evolution. By linking molecular-scale structural organization with population-scale evolutionary dynamics, we provide a mechanistic framework for understanding why distinct viruses exhibit markedly different antigenic trajectories. More broadly, these findings suggest that host receptor architecture itself may help define the range of evolutionarily accessible immune escape pathways available to a virus.

MATERIALS AND METHODSStructural data collection and multidimensional scaling

Structural data for viral binding proteins in complex with their respective receptors were retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) (53). For the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein, PDB IDs 7DX1, 7DX3, 7DX5, 7DX7, 7DX8, 7DX9, 7WVN, and 8HRI were utilized (54, 55). For the influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin (HA) protein, PDB IDs 2YP8, 4WEA, and 6TZB were used (16, 27, 56). For the influenza B HA protein, PDB ID 2RFU was used (57). Additionally, 4JTV and 6ACJ were utilized for H1N1pdm09 and SARS-CoV, respectively (34, 35). Structural visualization and mapping were performed using UCSF ChimeraX (v1.11) (58). To represent the spatial position of each residue, the 3D coordinates of the alpha carbons were extracted using our in-house script. For proteins comprising multiple chains or exhibiting multiple conformational states, the spatial coordinates of homologous sites were averaged across all chains and conformations prior to multidimensional scaling (MDS). The MDS spatial projection was conducted in R using the cmdscale function.

Collection of functional and structural indices

Deep mutational scanning (DMS) functional profiles were aggregated from multiple published studies (Table S1). Mutation-level yeast-display antibody escape scores and ACE2-binding affinities were calculated from original DMS data following our previously established pipeline (1, 9). Briefly, the antibody escape score was calculated by merging the mutational escape profiles of all isolated monoclonal antibodies, weighting each profile by its experimental neutralization titer in order to represent the selective pressure exerted by serum antibodies. Mutation-level pseudovirus-measured serum escape scores and Spike-mediated cell entry indices were directly obtained from data sets published by Bloom et al. (10, 11, 19, 28).

Because mutation-level DMS data typically encompass multiple data sets corresponding to different viral variants, we transformed mutation-level measurements into normalized site-specific mutational impact scores to evaluate structural sensitivity independently of lineage contexts. Within each data set, we first calculated the absolute value of the mutational effect for all 20 amino acid substitutions at each site (focusing on the magnitude of the impact rather than the directional sign) and then computed the mean. Each site was subsequently normalized against the maximum value observed across the entire Spike protein. To integrate multiple variant data sets, we assigned the maximum recorded normalized score to each residue across all variants. This approach minimizes biases introduced by uneven antibody distributions across different variant exposures, such as immunological imprinting, reflecting the potential contribution of each site.

Consequently, all derived site-specific impact scores in this analysis are positive, non-directional magnitudes. A higher impact score indicates that a given residue is highly sensitive to substitution, meaning mutations at this site exert a profound impact on the respective viral function.

Structural indices were calculated using an in-house Python script utilizing the Biopython package based on the PDB structures mentioned above. During the calculation of intrinsic structural properties, such as weighted contact number (WCN) and relative solvent accessibility (RSA), receptor chains were deliberately removed from the complexes. The 'distance to receptor' was defined as the minimum Euclidean distance from a given viral residue’s alpha-carbon to the alpha-carbon of any receptor residue.

Calculation of evolutionary indices

The phylogenetic mutation incidence, representing the number of independent mutational events (homoplasy), was calculated following our previously described methodology (1, 9). For SARS-CoV-2, the calculation utilizes the global phylogenetic tree from the UShER database (accessed 17 December 2025) (59). For influenza H3N2, all 56,741 complete human-host HA protein sequences collected in North America were retrieved from GISAID in December 2025 (60). Sequences were chronologically sorted and subjected to temporal equal-interval subsampling to construct a representative data set of 5,697 complete HA sequences. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic inference was performed using IQ-TREE (v1.6.12) (61) with default parameters and the optimal amino acid substitution model (Dayhoff + F + R5) selected automatically via ModelFinder. The tree was rooted using the historic ancestral strain A/Hong Kong/01/1968 as an outgroup.

Evolutionary leap events of SARS-CoV-2 were estimated by comparing each lineage to its direct ancestor (if documented on the Pango lineage website). Recombinants were excluded. Events involving >7 amino acid substitutions in the Spike protein were classified as “evolutionary leaps” (n = 13, total Spike mutations = 197), while those with <5 substitutions were classified as “stepwise” evolution (n = 2,003, total Spike mutations = 1,215).

The evolutionary rate was calculated by regression analysis, comparing the cumulative number of amino acid substitutions against sample collection dates across distance-defined regions from the receptor. Regression slopes were further normalized by the total number of amino acid residues within each respective spatial bin. For influenza H3N2, substitution counts were calculated relative to the A/Arizona/13/2010 strain, selected as the reference strain because its collection date represents the temporal midpoint of the sampled timeframe. Substitutions in strains collected prior to 2010 were assigned negative values to reduce bias from back-mutations and recurrent mutations. For SARS-CoV-2, the consensus sequence of each Pango lineage (total n = 2,068) was used. Substitution numbers were calculated relative to the Wuhan-Hu-1 reference genome.

Structure-based prediction of site competitiveness

To predict antigenic escape sites based on spatial steric hindrance, we developed a custom Python script. The algorithm quantifies the structural “competitiveness” of each viral residue, identifying surface sites where antibody binding would physically clash with the host receptor. For each viral residue, the algorithm centers a virtual sphere with a default radius of 45 Å on its alpha-carbon. In the case of receptor binding, the virtual sphere is located on the outer surface of the residue, oriented along the surface normal. In the case of ligand binding, the virtual sphere is centered on the alpha-carbon of each residue. It then calculates a “clash number” by counting the total number of receptor atoms located within this sphere, effectively simulating the steric bulk imposed by an antibody. To account for the baseline physical availability of the residue to antibodies, this clash number is multiplied by the residue’s solvent-accessibility surface area (SASA).

Machine learning prediction using EVEscape

To benchmark our structure-based competitiveness metric against generalized sequence-based machine learning approaches, we utilized the EVEscape model (18). For the influenza H3N2 HA protein, predictions were generated locally by running the official EVEscape pipeline with default parameters, using A/Massachusetts/18/2022 as the input sequence without any supplementary modifications or fine-tuning. For SARS-CoV-2, the EVEscape prediction scores for the Spike protein were directly retrieved from the pre-computed data sets published in the original EVEscape study.
